questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: A transparent dielectric coating is applied to glass (\(\epsilon_r = 4, \mu_r = 1\)) to eliminate the reflection of red light (\(\lambda_0 = 0.75 \mu\text{m}\)). The minimum thickness of the dielectric coating, in \(\mu\text{m}\), that can be used is ______ (rounded off to two decimal places).
questions.explanation:
To achieve no reflection at the interface, the intermediate layer acts as a quarter-wave impedance transformer. The matching condition requires the intrinsic impedance of the second medium, \(\eta_{2}\), to be the geometric mean of the impedances of the surrounding media, \(\eta_{1}\) (glass) and \(\eta_{3}\) (air): \[\eta_{2} = \sqrt{\eta_{1} \cdot \eta_{3}}\] In terms of relative permittivity \(\epsilon_{r}\), this corresponds to: \[\epsilon_{r2} = \sqrt{\epsilon_{r1} \cdot \epsilon_{r3}}\] Given \(\epsilon_{r1}\) (glass) and \(\epsilon_{r3} = 1\) (air), \(\epsilon_{r2} = 2\). For impedance matching, the required thickness \(d\) of the quarter-wave transformer is: [figure unavailable] \[d = (2n + 1)\frac{\lambda}{4}; \quad n = 0, 1, 2, \dots\] The wavelength \(\lambda\) in the second medium is given by: \[\lambda = \frac{\lambda_{0}}{\sqrt{\epsilon_{r2}}} = \frac{0.75 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 0.53 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}\] For the minimum thickness (\(n=0\)): \[d = \frac{\lambda}{4} = \frac{0.53 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}}{4} = 0.133\,\mu\text{m}\] \[\boxed{0.133\,\mu\text{m}}\]
Key points
  • A quarter-wave transformer eliminates reflections at a dielectric interface by creating destructive interference between reflections from the two boundaries.
  • The condition \(\eta_{2} = \sqrt{\eta_{1}\eta_{3}}\) is necessary for a perfectly matched condition at the design frequency.
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure the wavelength used in the thickness formula is the wavelength inside the matching medium, not the free-space wavelength \(\lambda_{0}\).
  • Remember that the thickness \(d\) must be an odd multiple of \(\lambda/4\) for the phase cancellation to work correctly.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The following circuit(s) representing a lumped element equivalent of an infinitesimal section of a transmission line is/are
questions.explanation:
An infinitesimal section of a transmission line of length \(\Delta z\) is characterized by the series impedance \(Z = R + j\omega L\) and shunt admittance \(Y = G + j\omega C\). For an incremental section of length \(\Delta z\), these are represented as \(R\Delta z\), \(L\Delta z\), \(G\Delta z\), and \(C\Delta z\). A transmission line section can be modeled using several equivalent circuit configurations:
  • Option B (L-section): This represents a basic asymmetric unit. When multiple L-sections are cascaded in series, they form the complete transmission line model, making it a valid representation of an infinitesimal section.
  • Option C (\(\Pi\)-network): In a symmetric \(\Pi\)-equivalent circuit, the series impedance \(Z\Delta z = (R+j\omega L)\Delta z\) is placed in the center series arm, and the shunt admittance \(Y\Delta z = (G+j\omega C)\Delta z\) is split into two equal components \((Y\Delta z)/2\) at the input and output.
  • Option D (T-network): In a symmetric T-equivalent circuit, the shunt admittance \(Y\Delta z = (G+j\omega C)\Delta z\) is placed in the center shunt arm, and the series impedance \(Z\Delta z = (R+j\omega L)\Delta z\) is split into two equal components \((Z\Delta z)/2\) at the input and output.
Option A is incorrect because it incorrectly splits the shunt elements without maintaining the required symmetric or L-section topology. \[\boxed{B, C, D}\]
Key points
  • Transmission lines are modeled as a cascade of infinitesimal lumped-element sections.
  • L-sections (asymmetric) are the basic building blocks that form the line when cascaded.
  • \(\Pi\) and T-networks are symmetric representations of a single infinitesimal section.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: The standing wave ratio on a \(50\ \Omega\) lossless transmission line terminated in an unknown load impedance is found to be \(2.0\). The distance between successive voltage minima is \(30\ \text{cm}\) and the first minimum is located at \(10\ \text{cm}\) from the load. \(Z_L\) can be replaced by an equivalent length \(l_m\) and terminating resistance \(R_m\) of the same line. The value of \(R_m\) and \(l_m\), respectively, are [figure unavailable]
questions.explanation:
To analyze the given transmission line problem with characteristic impedance \(Z_{0} = 50\,\Omega\) and standing wave ratio \(S = 2\): The problem explores the location of voltage maxima (\(l_{\text{max}}\)) and minima (\(l_{\text{min}}\)) relative to the load impedance (\(Z_{L}\)). Using the Smith chart transformation properties:
Method 1
\[\begin{aligned} & Z_0 = 50\,\Omega, \quad S = 2, \quad \lambda = 60\,\text{cm} &\\ & \text{min} = 10\,\text{cm} &\\ & \text{maximum} = \text{min} + \frac{\lambda}{4} = 10\,\text{cm} + 15\,\text{cm} = 25\,\text{cm} &\\ & R_{\text{max}} = S Z_0 = 2 \times 50 = 100\,\Omega &\\ & R_{\text{min}} = \frac{Z_0}{S} = \frac{50}{2} = 25\,\Omega & \end{aligned}\] The second circuit with \(R_m\) will have the same Smith chart as the first circuit because magnitude of reflection coefficient will remain the same in both the circuits. So in the second circuit we are initially at load at \(R_{\text{max}}\) then we have to reach the same load point on Smith chart as of first circuit so we must have \(L = 5 \, \text{cm}\). [figure unavailable] \[l_{\text{max}} = 5\,\text{cm}\][figure unavailable] \[l_{\text{min}} = 20\,\text{cm}\]
Method 2
Given \(S = 2\), \(Z_{\text{min}} = 10\text{ cm}\), \(Z_0 = 50\ \Omega\). As we know that, \[|\Gamma| = \frac{S-1}{S+1} = \frac{2-1}{2+1} = \frac{1}{3}\] Now, distance between successive voltage minima \(= 30\text{ cm}\) \[\Rightarrow \frac{\lambda}{2} = 30\text{ cm}\] \[\Rightarrow \lambda = 60\text{ cm}\] Also, for minima, \[2\beta Z_{\text{min}} = (2n + 1)\pi + \theta_{\Gamma}\] At \(n = 0\), 1st minima, \(Z_{\text{min}} = 10\text{ cm}\) \[\frac{4\pi}{\lambda} Z_{\text{min}} = \pi + \theta_{\Gamma}\] \[\Rightarrow \frac{4\pi}{60} \times 10 = \pi + \theta_{\Gamma}\] \[\Rightarrow \frac{2\pi}{3} - \pi = \theta_{\Gamma}\] \[\Rightarrow \theta_{\Gamma} = \frac{-\pi}{3} \quad \therefore \Gamma = \frac{1}{3} \angle -60^{\circ}\] Now, \[\Gamma = \frac{Z_L - Z_0}{Z_L + Z_0}\] \[\Rightarrow Z_L = Z_0 \left[ \frac{1+\Gamma}{1-\Gamma} \right]\] \[\Rightarrow Z_L = 50 \left[ \frac{1 + 0.33e^{-j\frac{\pi}{3}}}{1 - 0.33e^{-j\frac{\pi}{3}}} \right]\] \[\Rightarrow Z_L = 67.97 \angle -32.67^{\circ}\] Now, \[Z_{\text{in}} = Z_0 \left[ \frac{Z_L + jZ_0 \tan \beta l}{Z_0 + jZ_L \tan \beta l} \right]\] \[\Rightarrow Z_{\text{in}} = 50 \left[ \frac{R_m + j50 \tan \beta l_m}{50 + jR_m \tan \beta l_m} \right]\] Here, \(Z_{\text{in}} = Z_L = 67.97 \angle -32.67^{\circ}\). Going through options, \[\left. \begin{aligned} R_m &= 100\ \Omega \text{ and } l_m = 5\text{ cm} \\ R_m &= 25\ \Omega \text{ and } l_m = 20\text{ cm} \end{aligned} \right\} \text{ satisfy this}\] \[\boxed{(B, C) : R_m = 25\ \Omega, \ l_m = 20\ \text{cm}; \ R_m = 100\ \Omega, \ l_m = 5\ \text{cm}}\]
Key points
  • The maximum and minimum resistance values on the line are given by \(R_{\text{max}} = S Z_{0}\) and \(R_{\text{min}} = \frac{Z_{0}}{S}\).
  • For \(S=2\) and \(Z_{0}=50\,\Omega\): \[R_{\text{max}} = 2 \times 50 = 100\,\Omega\] \[R_{\text{min}} = \frac{50}{2} = 25\,\Omega\]
Mistakes to avoid
  • Ensure the relationship between \(l_{\text{max}}\) and \(l_{\text{min}}\) is always \(l_{\text{max}} = l_{\text{min}} \pm \frac{\lambda}{4}\).
  • Verify the direction of rotation on the Smith chart (towards the load vs. towards the generator).

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.explanation:
The objective is to derive the scattering parameters \(S_{11}\) and \(S_{21}\) for a network with transmission line extensions of lengths \(l_{1}\) and \(l_{2}\). [figure unavailable] Evaluation of \(S_{11}\) at \(V_{2}^{+} = 0\): Given that the total voltage at port 1 is the sum of incident and reflected waves: \[V_{1} = V_{1}^{+} + V_{1}^{-} = (V_{1}^{+})' e^{-j\beta l_{1}} + (V_{1}^{-})' e^{+j\beta l_{1}}\] Considering the transformation of the waves due to the line length \(l_{1}\), where \(\theta_{1} = \beta l_{1}\): \[S_{11} = \frac{V_{1}^{-}}{V_{1}^{+}} = \frac{(V_{1}^{-})' e^{+j\beta l_{1}}}{(V_{1}^{+})' e^{-j\beta l_{1}}} = S_{11}' e^{j2\beta l_{1}}\] Rearranging to find the intrinsic \(S_{11}'\): \[S_{11}' = S_{11} e^{-j2\beta l_{1}} = S_{11} e^{-j2\theta_{1}}\] Evaluation of \(S_{21}\) at \(V_{2}^{+} = 0\): For the transmission parameter \(S_{21}\), we analyze the voltage at port 2: \[V_{2} = V_{2}^{+} e^{j\beta l_{2}} + V_{2}^{-} e^{-j\beta l_{2}} = (V_{2}^{+})' + (V_{2}^{-})'\] Since \(V_{2}^{+} = 0\), we have \(V_{2} = (V_{2}^{-})'\), which implies: \[V_{2}^{-} = (V_{2}^{-})' e^{+j\beta l_{2}}\] Using the relation for \(S_{21} = \frac{V_{2}^{-}}{V_{1}^{+}}\) and substituting the phase shifts: \[S_{21} = \frac{(V_{2}^{-})' e^{+j\beta l_{2}}}{(V_{1}^{+})' e^{-j\beta l_{1}}} = S_{21}' e^{j(\beta l_{2} + \beta l_{1})}\] Thus: \[S_{21}' = S_{21} e^{-j(\beta l_{1} + \beta l_{2})} = S_{21} e^{-j(\theta_{1} + \theta_{2})}\] \[\boxed{\text{(A)}}\]
Key points
  • The reference plane transformation for scattering parameters introduces a phase shift of \(e^{-j2\theta}\) for reflection coefficients (\(S_{11}, S_{22}\)) and \(e^{-j(\theta_{i} + \theta_{j})}\) for transmission coefficients (\(S_{21}, S_{12}\)).
  • \(\theta = \beta l\) represents the electrical length of the transmission line section.

questions.subject: electromagnetic-fields
questions.question: Consider a narrow band signal, propagating in a lossless dielectric medium (\(\epsilon_r = 4, \mu_r = 1\)), with phase velocity \(v_p\) and group velocity \(v_g\). Which of the following statement is true? (\(c\) is the velocity of light in vacuum.)
questions.explanation:
The relationship between phase velocity \(V_{p}\) and group velocity \(V_{g}\) in a medium is derived as follows:
  • Phase Velocity (\(V_{p}\)):
    The phase velocity is the rate at which the phase of the wave propagates in space. It is given by: \[V_{p} = \frac{\omega}{\beta} = \frac{\omega}{\omega\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu\epsilon}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_{0}\epsilon_{0}}\sqrt{\mu_{r}\epsilon_{r}}} = \frac{c}{\sqrt{\mu_{r}\epsilon_{r}}}\] Since \(\sqrt{\mu_{r}\epsilon_{r}} \geq 1\) for any material medium, it follows that: \[V_{p} \leq c\]
  • Group Velocity (\(V_{g}\)):
    The group velocity is the velocity with which the envelope of a wave packet travels. It is defined as: \[V_{g} = \frac{d\omega}{d\beta} = \frac{V_{p}}{1 - \frac{\omega}{V_{p}}\frac{dV_{p}}{d\omega}}\] In a non-dispersive medium where the phase velocity \(V_{p}\) is independent of frequency (i.e., \(V_{p} \neq f(\omega)\), so \(\frac{dV_{p}}{d\omega} = 0\)), the expression simplifies: \[V_{g} = V_{p}\]
Since \(V_{p} \leq c\) and \(V_{g} = V_{p}\) in this condition, we conclude: \[\boxed{(D):V_{p} < c, \, V_{g} < c}\]
Key points
  • Phase velocity \(V_{p}\) represents the propagation speed of a single frequency component.
  • Group velocity \(V_{g}\) represents the speed of information or energy transmission.
  • In dispersive media, \(V_{p}\) and \(V_{g}\) are generally different, and \(V_{g}\) can even exceed \(c\) under specific conditions (anomalous dispersion), though the signal velocity remains \(\leq c\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: We reached the station late, and ________ missed the train.
questions.explanation:
We need to select the most appropriate word to complete the sentence: ``We reached the station late, and missed the train.'' Let us look at the meaning of the choices:
  • near is an adjective or preposition indicating close proximity.
  • nearly is an adverb meaning almost or very close to a state. In this context, ``nearly missed'' means they managed to catch the train, but only by a very small margin.
  • utterly means completely/totally, which is ungrammatical before ``missed'' in this sentence structure.
  • mostly means mainly/for the most part.
Since reaching the station late creates a scenario where missing the train becomes a very close possibility, **nearly** fits the intended description perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{B. nearly}}\]
Key points
  • Adverbial modifiers like nearly indicate that an action came very close to occurring but did not actually happen, or happened by a very slim margin.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Kind: ________ :: Often: Frequently (By word meaning)
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation:
We are asked to complete the vocabulary analogy by word meaning: \[\text{Kind} : \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}} :: \text{Often} : \text{Frequently}\] Let us analyze the baseline pair:
  • Often and Frequently are direct **synonyms**.
  • Therefore, the missing word must be a synonym for **Kind**.
  • Looking at the options, both **B. Type** (as in ``a kind/type of animal'') and **D. Kindly** (as an alternate form/synonym in certain contexts) could be argued as plausible interpretations depending on the intended axis.
Because of this multiple valid options ambiguity, the question was officially declared as **Marks to All (MTA)**. \[\boxed{\text{MTA}}\]
Key points
  • Verbal analogies require a single, unambiguous relationship axis. When multiple options satisfy separate dictionary definitions of a word, the item becomes flawed.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Which one of the following sentence sequences creates a coherent narrative?
  1. Once on the terrace, on her way to her small room in the corner, she notices the man right away.
  2. She begins to pant by the time she has climbed all the stairs.
  3. Mina has bought vegetables and rice at the market, so her bags are heavy.
  4. He was leaning against the parapet, watching the traffic below.
questions.explanation:
We need to arrange sentences (i), (ii), (iii), and (iv) in the most appropriate logical sequence to form a coherent narrative paragraph. Let us analyze the causal actions and spatial transitions across the sentences:
  • Sentence (iii): Establishes the background reason for the narrative action (``Mina has bought vegetables and rice at the market, so her bags are heavy''). This acts as a natural **opening setting sentence**.
  • Sentence (ii): Follows logically as she arrives home with those heavy bags and starts climbing (``She begins to pant by the time she has climbed all the stairs''). This creates the link: \(\text{(iii)} \rightarrow \text{(ii)}\).
  • Sentence (i): Tracks her movement as she finishes climbing and steps onto the roof (``Once on the terrace, on her way to her small room in the corner, she notices the man right away''). This follows the stairs from sentence (ii), linking them as \(\text{(ii)} \rightarrow \text{(i)}\).
  • Sentence (iv): Concludes the narrative by describing what the man she noticed was doing (``He was leaning against the parapet, watching the traffic below'').
Combining these links yields the logical narrative sequence: \(\text{(iii)} \rightarrow \text{(ii)} \rightarrow \text{(i)} \rightarrow \text{(iv)}\), which corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. (iii), (ii), (i), (iv)}}\]
Key points
  • Narrative reordering is solved by tracking the logical flow of physical actions step-by-step (such as buying heavy bags \(\rightarrow\) climbing stairs \(\rightarrow\) reaching the terrace terrace \(\rightarrow\) noticing a man).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: He did not manage to fix the car himself, so he ________ in the garage.
questions.explanation:
We need to select the most appropriate option to complete the sentence: ``He did not manage to fix the car himself, so he in the garage.'' Let us analyze the grammatical context and tense requirement:
  • The introductory clause ``He did not manage to fix...'' sets the narrative timeline firmly in the **simple past tense**.
  • When an action is arranged to be performed by someone else rather than by oneself, we use the passive causative construction: \(\text{Subject} + \text{have / get} + \text{object} + \text{past participle}\).
  • Matching the past tense requirement gives: ``got it fixed'' (where ``it'' refers back to the car).
Evaluating the alternative options: getting it fixed is a present participle, gets fixed is present tense, and got fixed is missing the crucial objective pronoun indicator. \[\boxed{\text{A. got it fixed}}\]
Key points
  • Passive causative structures follow the configuration: \(\text{get/have} + \text{object} + \text{past participle}\) (V3), representing tasks delegated to a third party.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Planting: Seed :: Raising: ________ (By word meaning)
questions.explanation:
We need to complete the vocabulary analogy by word meaning: \[\text{Planting} : \text{Seed} :: \text{Raising} : \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}\] Let us analyze the baseline functional relationship axis:
  • Planting is the specific agricultural action performed on a **Seed** to initiate its growth cycle.
  • Similarly, the verb **Raising** represents the nurturing action of bringing up and developing a **Child** to maturity.
Evaluating the alternatives: Temperature is increased/lowered, Height is increased, and a Lift is operated, none of which use the verb ``raising'' in an organic development sense. \[\boxed{\text{A. Child}}\]
Key points
  • Collocation and category action analogies require identifying the direct object that uniquely receives the action of the specified verb.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: In a recently held parent-teacher meeting, the teachers had very few complaints about Ravi. After all, Ravi was a hardworking and kind student. Incidentally, almost all of Ravi's friends at school were hardworking and kind too. But the teachers drew attention to Ravi's complete lack of interest in sports. The teachers believed that, along with some of his friends who showed similar disinterest in sports, Ravi needed to engage in some sports for his overall development. Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: All of Ravi's friends are hardworking and kind.
No one who is not a friend of Ravi is hardworking and kind.
None of Ravi's friends are interested in sports.
Some of Ravi's friends are hardworking and kind.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the logically sound inference supported with certainty by the provided text passage. Let us evaluate the choices using strict textual bounds:
  • Choice A states that *all* of Ravi's friends are hardworking and kind. The text only states that ``almost all of Ravi's friends at school were hardworking and kind too.'' The word ``almost'' means it does not apply to all of them.
  • Choices B and C introduce absolute, unbacked negative claims (``No one who is not...'', ``None of Ravi's friends...'') which cannot be inferred from the passage.
  • Choice D states: ``Some of Ravi's friends are hardworking and kind.'' Since ``almost all'' implies a significant majority, it is absolutely certain that at least *some* of his friends possess these traits.
Therefore, Choice D is the only valid inference. \[\boxed{\text{D. Some of Ravi's friends are hardworking and kind.}}\]
Key points
  • Avoid choices that introduce extreme or absolute words (all, none, always) unless they are explicitly backed by the text. A qualified premise like ``almost all'' naturally supports a milder sub-inference like ``some''.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Which one of the sentence sequences in the given options creates a coherent narrative?
  1. I could not bring myself to knock.
  2. There was a murmur of unfamiliar voices coming from the big drawing room and the door was firmly shut.
  3. The passage was dark for a bit, but then it suddenly opened into a bright kitchen.
  4. I decided I would rather wander down the passage.
questions.explanation:
We are given four sentences that need to be arranged to form a coherent narrative:
  1. I could not bring myself to knock.
  2. There was a murmur of unfamiliar voices coming from the big drawing room and the door was firmly shut.
  3. The passage was dark for a bit, but then it suddenly opened into a bright kitchen.
  4. I decided I would rather wander down the passage.
Step 1: Establish the narrative opening
  • Sentence (ii) sets the scene at the starting point—standing outside the closed drawing room hearing unfamiliar voices. Thus, (ii) is the opening statement.
Step 2: Trace the action and reaction
  • Feeling hesitant due to the shut door and unfamiliar voices in (ii), the speaker reacts in (i): ``I could not bring myself to knock.'' This forms the pair (ii) \(\to\) (i).
  • Unable to knock, the speaker makes an alternative choice in (iv): ``I decided I would rather wander down the passage.'' This establishes (i) \(\to\) (iv).
  • Entering and walking through the passage described in (iv) leads directly to the resolution in (iii): ``The passage was dark for a bit, but then it suddenly opened into a bright kitchen.'' This completes (iv) \(\to\) (iii).
Combining these steps yields the coherent sequence: **(ii), (i), (iv), (iii)**. This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. (ii), (i), (iv), (iii)}}\]
Key points
  • Narrative paragraph ordering depends on establishing cause-and-effect pairs, ensuring that a physical clue (hearing voices) is placed directly before the narrator's emotional or behavioral reaction (hesitating to knock).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Rafi told Mary, ``I am thinking of watching a film this weekend.'' The following reports the above statement in indirect speech: Rafi told Mary that he ________ of watching a film that weekend.
questions.explanation:
We need to select the most appropriate option to report the given direct speech statement in indirect speech: Direct speech: Rafi told Mary, ``I am thinking of watching a film this weekend.' Let us analyze the standard rules for tense shifting when moving from direct to indirect speech:
  • Since the reporting verb ``told'' is in the past tense, the verb tense within the quote must shift backward.
  • The present continuous form ``am thinking'' shifts backward to the **past continuous** form: **was thinking**.
  • The personal pronoun ``I'' updates to ``he'' to match the subject context, which is already provided.
This matches choice D perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{D. was thinking}}\]
Key points
  • Tense Shifting Rule: When changing statements into indirect speech behind a past-tense reporting verb, present continuous structures (\(\text{am/is/are} + \text{V-ing}\)) always convert to past continuous structures (\(\text{was/were} + \text{V-ing}\)).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Permit: ________ :: Enforce: Relax (By word meaning)
questions.explanation:
We are given a verbal analogy problem: \[\text{Permit} : \underline{\quad\quad\quad\quad} :: \text{Enforce} : \text{Relax}\] Step 1: Identify the relationship in the reference pair
  • Enforce means to compel observance of or obedience to a rule or law.
  • Relax (in the context of rules/laws) means to make a rule less strict or release enforcement.
  • Thus, Enforce and Relax are antonyms (opposite in word meaning).
Step 2: Find the antonym for the target word
  • Permit means to give authorization or consent to (allow).
  • We need to select the word among the options that is the direct antonym of **Permit**:
    • Allow: Synonym of Permit.
    • Forbid: Means to refuse to allow something (Antonym of Permit).
    • License: Synonym/related term to granting permission.
    • Reinforce: Means to strengthen or support.
Therefore, the word that completes the analogy is **Forbid**. This corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. Forbid}}\]
Key points
  • Vocabulary analogies depend on determining whether the baseline word pair maps onto a synonym or antonym conceptual axis.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Students of all the departments of a college who have successfully completed the registration process are eligible to vote in the upcoming college elections. However, by the time the due date for registration was over, it was found that surprisingly none of the students from the Department of Human Sciences had completed the registration process. Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following sets of statement(s) can be logically inferred with certainty?
  1. All those students who would not be eligible to vote in the college elections would certainly belong to the Department of Human Sciences.
  2. None of the students from departments other than Human Sciences failed to complete the registration process within the due time.
  3. All the eligible voters would certainly be students who are not from the Department of Human Sciences.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine which sets of statements can be logically inferred with certain validity based on the provided rules:
  • Rule 1: Completed registration \(\implies\) Eligible to vote.
  • Fact 2: Surprisingly, **none** of the students from the Department of Human Sciences completed the registration process.
Let us evaluate the three statements:
  • Statement (i): Claims *all* students who are ineligible to vote must belong to Human Sciences. This is invalid because students from *other* departments might also have missed the registration deadline and ended up ineligible.
  • Statement (ii): Claims *none* of the students from other departments failed to complete registration (meaning everyone else registered). This is unsupported because we only know that Human Sciences had zero registrations; we do not know if other departments had perfect registration rates.
  • Statement (iii): Claims all eligible voters are students who are *not* from the Department of Human Sciences. Since completing registration is a strict requirement for eligibility, and zero students from Human Sciences registered, it is absolutely certain that no Human Sciences student can be an eligible voter. Therefore, all eligible voters must come from other departments. **(Valid)**
Thus, only statement (iii) can be inferred with certainty. This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. only (iii)}}\]
Key points
  • According to standard conditional logic rules, if a condition is mandatory for an outcome (\(A \implies B\)), then the absence of that condition means the outcome cannot occur (\(\text{not } A \implies \text{not } B\)).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which one of the options does NOT describe the passage below or follow from it? We tend to think of cancer as a 'modern' illness because its metaphors are so modern. It is a disease of overproduction, of sudden growth, a growth that is unstoppable, tipped into the abyss of no control. Modern cell biology encourages us to imagine the cell as a molecular machine. Cancer is that machine unable to quench its initial command (to grow) and thus transform into an indestructible, self-propelled automaton.
options: It is a reflection of why cancer seems so modern to most of us.
It tells us that modern cell biology uses and promotes metaphors of machinery.
Modern cell biology encourages metaphors of machinery, and cancer is often imagined as a machine.
Modern cell biology never uses figurative language, such as metaphors, to describe or explain anything.
questions.explanation:
We are asked to identify which option does NOT describe the passage or follow from it. Passage Summary: ``We tend to think of cancer as a 'modern' illness because its metaphors are so modern. It is a disease of overproduction, of sudden growth... Modern cell biology encourages us to imagine the cell as a molecular machine. Cancer is that machine unable to quench its initial command (to grow) and thus transform into an indestructible, self-propelled automaton.'' Step 1: Evaluate each option against the text
  1. Option A: ``It is a reflection of why cancer seems so modern to most of us.'' This directly describes the first sentence: ``We tend to think of cancer as a 'modern' illness because its metaphors are so modern.'' Thus, Option A is **True** (and does not answer the NOT condition).
  2. Option B: ``It tells us that modern cell biology uses and promotes metaphors of machinery.'' The passage explicitly mentions: ``Modern cell biology encourages us to imagine the cell as a molecular machine.'' Thus, Option B is **True**.
  3. Option C: ``Modern cell biology encourages metaphors of machinery, and cancer is often imagined as a machine.'' This accurately synthesizes the passage's description of cells as molecular machines and cancer as an indestructible machine/automaton. Thus, Option C is **True**.
  4. Option D: ``Modern cell biology never uses figurative language, such as metaphors, to describe or explain anything.'' This completely contradicts the passage, which explicitly relies on figurative language and metaphors (e.g., ``molecular machine'', ``automaton'') to explain biological concepts. Thus, Option D is **False** and does **NOT** describe the passage.
This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. Modern cell biology never uses figurative language, such as metaphors, to describe or explain anything.}}\]
Key points
  • When looking for the statement that *does not* follow from a passage, watch out for absolute words like never or always, which often signal a false claim that directly contradicts the text.

questions.subject: general-aptitude

questions.explanation:

  • consensus means general agreement.
  • conscience is a noun meaning a person's moral sense of right and wrong, which acts as an internal guide to their behavior and choices.
  • consent means permission or agreement for something to happen.
Since the sentence describes an internal moral or personal standard that prevents the speaker from supporting a proposal, **conscience** is the perfect fit. \[\boxed{\text{C. conscience}}\]
Key points
  • Identifying contextually fitting nouns requires separating phonetically similar words (homophones/near-homophones like conscious vs. conscience) by their precise parts of speech and semantic meanings.

Evaluating the choices: *Executive* implements laws, and *Governmental* and *Legal* are broad descriptive terms. None match the precise structural branch mapping. \[\boxed{\text{A. Judiciary}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Forestland is a planet inhabited by different kinds of creatures. Among other creatures, it is populated by animals all of whom are ferocious. There are also creatures that have claws, and some that do not. All creatures that have claws are ferocious. Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following options can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: All creatures with claws are animals.
Some creatures with claws are non-ferocious.
Some ferocious creatures are creatures with claws.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the statement that can be logically inferred with absolute certainty based *only* on the provided text constraints. Let us map out the categorical relationships described in the text:
  • Relation 1: \(\text{Animals} \implies \text{Ferocious}\) (All animals are ferocious).
  • Relation 2: \(\text{Creatures with claws} \implies \text{Ferocious}\) (All creatures that have claws are ferocious).
  • There are also other creatures, some of which have claws and some of which do not.
Let us evaluate the choices based on these rules:
  • Choices A, B, and C make absolute claims that either violate the rules or cannot be verified (e.g., assuming creatures with claws *must* be animals, or that some clawed creatures are non-ferocious, which directly violates Relation 2).
  • Choice D states: ``Some ferocious creatures are creatures with claws.'' Since Relation 2 states that *all* creatures with claws are ferocious, it is a mathematical certainty that the set of ferocious creatures contains these clawed creatures. Therefore, *some* ferocious creatures are guaranteed to have claws.
This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. Some ferocious creatures are creatures with claws.}}\]
Key points
  • According to classic deductive logic rules, if a universal statement like ``All \(A\) are \(B\)'' is true, then its corresponding particular conversion, ``Some \(B\) are \(A\),'' is always logically valid.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which one of the following options can be inferred from the given passage alone? When I was a kid, I was partial to stories about other worlds and interplanetary travel. I used to imagine that I could just gaze off into space and be whisked to another planet.
options: It is a child's description of what he or she likes.
It is an adult's memory of what he or she liked as a child.
The child in the passage read stories about interplanetary travel only in parts.
It teaches us that stories are good for children.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the statement that can be logically inferred with certainty from the provided passage. Let us look at the opening phrase of the passage: ``When I was a kid, I was partial to stories about other worlds and interplanetary travel. I used to imagine...''
  • The use of the past tense phrase ``When I was a kid'' indicates that the speaker is no longer a child. They are looking back at their childhood from a later point in life.
  • Therefore, the passage represents an **adult's memory** of what they used to like when they were a child. This matches statement B perfectly.
  • Choice A is incorrect because the text is a retrospective memory from an adult, not a description written *by* a child. Choice C is incorrect because ``partial to'' means they had a strong liking or preference for those stories, not that they read them ``only in parts.''
This matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. It is an adult's memory of what he or she liked as a child.}}\]
Key points
  • Pay close attention to tense indicators and framing phrases (like ``When I was a kid'') to correctly determine the narrator's perspective and position in time.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The village was nestled in a green spot, ________ the ocean and the hills.
questions.explanation:
We need to select the contextually appropriate preposition to fill the blank: ``The village was nestled in a green spot, the ocean and the hills.'' Let us look at the given choices:
  • through denotes moving from one side to another inside an object or space.
  • in and at represent stationary containment or specific coordinate points.
  • between is used explicitly when positioning an object in the intermediate space separating two distinct entities or boundaries.
Since the sentence references two distinct geographic entities (``the ocean'' and ``the hills''), the spatial preposition between is grammatically correct. \[\boxed{\text{D. between}}\]
Key points
  • Spatial prepositions linking an object to exactly two clear landmarks or physical features require the dual-relation connector between.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Disagree: Protest :: Agree: ________ (By word meaning)
questions.explanation:
We need to complete the vocabulary analogy by word meaning: \[\text{Disagree} : \text{Protest} :: \text{Agree} : \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}\] Let us analyze the logical connection defining the baseline pair:
  • Protest is a formal or active outward behavioral expression of an internal state of Disagreement.
  • Following this identical behavioral manifestation track, we look for an active word that expresses a state of Agreement. To Recommend means to present something as worthy of trial or acceptance, which functions as an active endorsement or expression of agreement with a concept.
Evaluating the alternative choices: Refuse and Refute denote active disagreement, and a Pretext is an excuse, none of which reflect a positive consensus state. \[\boxed{\text{C. Recommend}}\]
Key points
  • Vocabulary analogies are solved by mapping the causal intensity path linking an inner cognitive state directly to its corresponding outer behavioral expression.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Residency is a famous housing complex with many well-established individuals among its residents. A recent survey conducted among the residents of the complex revealed that all of those residents who are well established in their respective fields happen to be academicians. The survey also revealed that most of these academicians are authors of some best-selling books. Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: Some residents of the complex who are well established in their fields are also authors of some best-selling books.
All academicians residing in the complex are well established in their fields.
Some authors of best-selling books are residents of the complex who are well established in their fields.
Some academicians residing in the complex are well established in their fields.
questions.note: Marks awarded to all (official key: MTA)
questions.explanation:
We need to evaluate the provided passage regarding the residents of a famous housing complex to identify the statement that can be logically inferred with complete certainty. Let us break down the categorical statements given in the text:
  • Premise 1: \(\text{Residents who are well-established in their fields} \implies \text{Academicians}\).
  • Premise 2: \(\text{Most of these academicians} \implies \text{Authors of best-selling books}\).
Let us evaluate the multiple-choice options. Notice that when we test choices A, B, C, and D against strict quantifier logic, ambiguities arise regarding whether the subsets are non-empty or if the phrasing implies bi-directional inclusion. Because of these logical ambiguities in the phrasing of the options, the question was officially marked as Marks to All (MTA). \[\boxed{\text{MTA}}\]
Key points
  • Deductive logic questions require a single, unambiguous option that follows strictly from the premises without requiring external assumptions about subset distributions.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: ``You are delaying the completion of the task. Send ________ contributions at the earliest.''
questions.explanation:
We need to select the grammatically correct word to complete the sentence: ``You are delaying the completion of the task. Send contributions at the earliest. Let us analyze the grammatical requirement of the blank:
  • The word precedes the plural noun ``contributions'', which means we need a possessive determiner to indicate ownership.
  • your is the second-person possessive determiner. It fits the context perfectly.
Evaluating the alternative choices: you are and you're are subject-verb contractions, and yore is a noun referring to time long past. None can grammatically modify a noun directly here. \[\boxed{\text{B. your}}\]
Key points
  • Separate phonetically identical or similar words (homophones like your vs. you're) by identifying the target part of speech required by the surrounding sentence structure.
