questions.explanation:
We need to complete the vocabulary analogy by word meaning: \[\underline{\hspace{1.5cm}} : \text{Guidelines} :: \text{Implement} : \text{References}\] Let us analyze the contextual relationship defining the baseline reference pair:
  • The pair on the right sets up an action-object relationship: you Implement an operational plan based on Guidelines, or rather, let's reverse look at the word pairing. To Cite means to quote or refer to References in an academic context.
  • Following this structural logic, the word Cite is a precise verb that acts upon research citations or references.
Evaluating the alternative homophones: Sight refers to vision, Site refers to a physical location, and Plagiarise means to copy illegally without attribution. \[\boxed{\text{C. Cite}}\]
Key points
  • Academic vocabulary analogies are resolved by identifying the precise technical verb that defines standard research or operational actions on documentation objects.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: In 2022, June Huh was awarded the Fields medal, which is the highest prize in Mathematics. When he was younger, he was also a poet. He did not win any medals in the International Mathematics Olympiads. He dropped out of college. Based only on the above information, which one of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: Every Fields medalist has won a medal in an International Mathematics Olympiad.
Everyone who has dropped out of college has won the Fields medal.
All Fields medalists are part-time poets.
Some Fields medalists have dropped out of college.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine which statement can be logically inferred with complete certainty based *only* on the provided text passage about June Huh. Let us summarize the concrete factual assertions given in the text:
  • June Huh was awarded the Fields Medal in 2026.
  • When he was younger, he was also a poet.
  • He did not win any medals in the International Mathematical Olympiad (IMO).
  • He dropped out of college.
Let us evaluate the choices against these rules:
  • Choices A, B, and C turn a specific detail about a single individual into a sweeping generalization about *all* Fields medalists (e.g., assuming *every* medalist won an IMO or that *all* of them are part-time poets). These are logical fallacies.
  • Choice D states: ``Some Fields medalists have dropped out of college.'' Since June Huh is a Fields medalist, and he dropped out of college, it is an absolute factual certainty that at least *some* (meaning at least one) member of the Fields medalist category matches this description.
\[\boxed{\text{D. Some Fields medalists have dropped out of college.}}\]
Key points
  • Universal generalizations (\(\forall x\)) cannot be inferred from a single sample point. However, a single positive instance (\(A \in X\) and \(A \in Y\)) is completely sufficient to validate an existential particular inference (\(\exists x \in X\) such that \(x \in Y\)).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Human beings are one among many creatures that inhabit an imagined world. In this imagined world, some creatures are cruel. If in this imagined world, it is given that the statement ``Some human beings are not cruel creatures'' is FALSE, then which of the following set of statement(s) can be logically inferred with certainty?
  1. All human beings are cruel creatures.
  2. Some human beings are cruel creatures.
  3. Some creatures that are cruel are human beings.
  4. No human beings are cruel creatures.
questions.explanation:
We are given the following logical conditions within an imagined world context:
  • Premise: The specific statement ``Some human beings are not cruel creatures'' is FALSE.
We need to identify which of the numbered sub-statements can be logically inferred with absolute certainty based on this premise. Let us evaluate the truth values using standard categorical proposition logic rules:
  1. The statement ``Some \(H\) are not \(C\)'' is a particular negative proposition (O-proposition).
  2. According to the classical square of opposition rules, if an O-proposition is completely false, then its direct diagonal contradictory partner—the universal affirmative statement (A-proposition), ``All \(H\) are \(C\)''—must be absolutely TRUE.
  3. Therefore, statement (i), ``All human beings are cruel creatures,'' is guaranteed to be true.
  4. Since all human beings are cruel, it follows directly that any subset of human beings must also be cruel. This makes statement (ii), ``Some human beings are cruel creatures,'' also true.
  5. Similarly, since these human beings are cruel, the intersection group of cruel creatures must include them, which makes statement (iii), ``Some creatures that are cruel are human beings,'' also true.
Thus, statements (i), (ii), and (iii) are all logically sound inferences. This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. (i), (ii) and (iii)}}\]
Key points
  • According to standard categorical logic rules, proving a particular negative statement (\(\exists x \in H\) such that \(x \notin C\)) false automatically validates its universal affirmative contradiction (\(\forall x \in H, x \in C\)).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The World Bank has declared that it does not plan to offer new financing to Sri Lanka, which is battling its worst economic crisis in decades, until the country has an adequate macroeconomic policy framework in place. In a statement, the World Bank said Sri Lanka needed to adopt structural reforms that focus on economic stabilisation and tackle the root causes of its crisis. The latter has starved it of foreign exchange and led to shortages of food, fuel, and medicines. The bank is repurposing resources under existing loans to help alleviate shortages of essential items such as medicine, cooking gas, fertiliser, meals for children, and cash for vulnerable households. Based only on the above passage, which one of the following statements can be inferred with certainty?
options: According to the World Bank, the root cause of Sri Lanka's economic crisis is that it does not have enough foreign exchange.
The World Bank has stated that it will advise the Sri Lankan government about how to tackle the root causes of its economic crisis.
According to the World Bank, Sri Lanka does not yet have an adequate macroeconomic policy framework.
The World Bank has stated that it will provide Sri Lanka with additional funds for essentials such as food, fuel, and medicines.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify which statement can be inferred with certain validity based *only* on the provided text passage regarding the World Bank and Sri Lanka. Let us evaluate the choices against explicit textual bounds:
  • Choices A, B, and D make absolute claims or suggest policy actions that are not supported by the passage (such as claiming the World Bank *has already stated* it will provide additional funding, when the text notes it *does not plan* to offer new financing until an adequate macroeconomic framework is in place).
  • Choice C states: ``According to the World Bank, Sri Lanka does not yet have an adequate macroeconomic policy framework.'' This is directly supported by the text, which explicitly states that the World Bank does not plan to offer new financing ``until the country has an adequate macroeconomic policy framework in place.'' This conditional phrasing clearly shows that such a framework is currently missing.
This matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C}}\]
Key points
  • Valid reading comprehension inferences are found by looking at conditional statements (like ``not until \(X\) is in place'') to deduce the current true status of a situation.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which one of the following shapes can be used to tile (completely cover by repeating) a flat plane, extending to infinity in all directions, without leaving any empty spaces in between them? The copies of the shape used to tile are identical and are not allowed to overlap.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine which shape among a circle, regular octagon, regular pentagon, and rhombus can be used to form a valid, continuous regular tessellation that tiles a flat plane to infinity without leaving any empty gaps or overlapping. Let us analyze the interior angle constraints required for regular polygons to tessellate a flat plane:
  • For a shape to tile a plane perfectly without gaps, the sum of the interior angles of the shapes meeting at any vertex point must add up to exactly \(360^\circ\). This means the interior angle of the shape must be an exact integer divisor of \(360^\circ\).
  • Circles (A): Curved edges cannot form flat edges, leaving gaps automatically.
  • Regular Pentagons (C): The interior angle is \(108^\circ\). Since \(360 \div 108 = 3.33\) (not an integer), pentagons cannot tile a plane.
  • Regular Octagons (B): The interior angle is \(135^\circ\). Since \(360 \div 135 = 2.67\) (not an integer), octagons cannot tile a plane on their own without leaving square gaps.
  • Rhombus (D): A rhombus is a quadrilateral. The interior angles of any arbitrary quadrilateral always sum to \(360^\circ\). By rotating and matching their sides, any quadrilateral shape can tile a flat plane perfectly to infinity without leaving any gaps.
Therefore, a rhombus can successfully tile the plane. This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. rhombus}}\]
Key points
  • Planar Tessellation Rule: While only three regular polygons (triangles, squares, and hexagons) can tile a plane on their own, any general quadrilateral shape (including an asymmetric quadrilateral or a rhombus) can tile a flat plane perfectly because its interior angles sum to \(360^\circ\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: ``I have not yet decided what I will do this evening; I ________ visit a friend.''
questions.explanation:
We need to select the most appropriate modal auxiliary verb to complete the sentence: ``I have not yet decided what I will do this evening; I visit a friend. Let us evaluate the choices based on grammatical meaning:
  • mite is a noun referring to a tiny arachnid or a small amount of money, which is contextually irrelevant.
  • would expresses a definite intention, habit, or conditional certainty, which contradicts the opening statement ``I have not yet decided.''
  • might is a modal verb used to express a weak possibility or uncertainty regarding a future action. It fits the speaker's undecided state perfectly.
  • didn't is a past-tense negative auxiliary that is grammatically incompatible with the future timeframe of ``this evening.''
Since the speaker has not finalized their plans, the choice must express possibility, making might the correct choice. \[\boxed{\text{C. might}}\]
Key points
  • When a clause explicitly introduces a state of indecision or lack of certainty (e.g., ``not yet decided''), the subsequent clause requires a modal verb of possibility like might or may.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Eject: Insert :: Advance: ________ (By word meaning)
questions.explanation:
We need to complete the vocabulary analogy by word meaning: \[\text{Eject} : \text{Insert} :: \text{Advance} : \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}}\] Let us analyze the relationship defining the baseline reference pair:
  • Eject (to force or throw something out) and Insert (to place or put something in) are direct antonyms.
  • Following this identical structural rule, we look for the direct antonym of Advance (to move forward or make progress).
  • The word Retreat means to move back or withdraw from a position, which serves as the perfect opposite of advance.
Evaluating the alternative choices: Advent means an arrival, Progress is a synonym, and Loan is a financial transaction. None fit the antonym axis. \[\boxed{\text{C. Retreat}}\]
Key points
  • Vocabulary analogies require identifying the precise semantic axis (synonyms, antonyms, cause-effect) of the first pair and reproducing it exactly for the second pair.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A duck named Donald Duck says ``All ducks always lie.'' Based only on the information above, which one of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: Donald Duck always tells the truth.
questions.explanation:
A duck named Donald Duck says: ``All ducks always lie.'' We need to find which statement can be logically inferred with absolute certainty based *only* on this information. Let us analyze the truth value of Donald Duck's statement using case analysis:
  • Suppose Donald Duck's statement is true. This would mean that *all* ducks always lie, which includes Donald Duck himself since he is a duck. Therefore, Donald Duck's statement must be a lie (false). This creates a logical contradiction.
  • Now, suppose Donald Duck's statement is false. This implies that it is not true that *all* ducks always lie, meaning at least some ducks sometimes tell the truth. This assumption does not create any logical contradictions.
Since the statement cannot be true without creating a contradiction, it must be false. This makes Statement D mathematically certain. \[\boxed{\text{D. Donald Duck's statement is false.}}\]
Key points
  • Self-referential universal claims of deception (such as ``Everyone always lies'') are logically impossible to validate as true, meaning the statement itself must be false under classical logic rules.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Based only on the truth of the statement `Some humans are intelligent', which one of the following options can be logically inferred with certainty?
questions.explanation:
We are given that the statement ``Some humans are intelligent'' is completely TRUE. We need to determine which choice can be logically inferred from this with absolute certainty. Let us evaluate the choices using strict categorical logic rules:
  • The statement ``Some \(H\) are \(I\)'' is a particular affirmative statement (I-proposition).
  • Choices A and B make sweeping universal claims (``No human is...'', ``All humans are...'') that cannot be proven from a limited particular statement.
  • Choice C discusses non-humans, which falls completely outside the scope of our premise.
  • Choice D states: ``Some intelligent beings are humans.'' In formal logic, a particular affirmative statement (I-proposition) can always be converted directly by swapping its subject and predicate terms (\(P \cap S = S \cap P\)). If some humans are intelligent, it is a mathematical certainty that some intelligent beings are humans.
Therefore, Choice D is the only logically sound inference. \[\boxed{\text{D. Some intelligent beings are humans.}}\]
Key points
  • Direct Conversion Law: Particular affirmative statements (\(\exists x \text{ such that } x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\)) are perfectly symmetrical, meaning they can always be converted directly without changing their truth value.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
The James Webb telescope, recently launched in space, is giving humankind unprecedented access to the depths of time by imaging very old stars formed almost 13 billion years ago. Astrophysicists and cosmologists believe that this odyssey in space may even shed light on the existence of dark matter. Dark matter is supposed to interact only via the gravitational interaction and not through the electromagnetic-, the weak- or the strong-interaction. This may justify the epithet "dark" in dark matter.
Based on the above paragraph, which one of the following statements is FALSE?
options: No other telescope has captured images of stars older than those captured by the James Webb telescope.
People other than astrophysicists and cosmologists may also believe in the existence of dark matter.
The James Webb telescope could be of use in the research on dark matter.
If dark matter was known to interact via the strong-interaction, then the epithet "dark" would be justified.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify which statement is FALSE based *only* on the provided passage about the James Webb telescope and dark matter. Let us evaluate each choice using strict textual boundaries:
  • Choices A, B, and C reflect information supported by the text or state plausible sub-inferences that do not contradict it (such as noting that cosmologists believe this odyssey may shed light on dark matter).
  • Choice D states: ``If dark matter was known to interact via the strong-interaction, then the epithet 'dark' would be justified.'' This completely contradicts the passage, which explicitly states that dark matter is called ``dark'' precisely because it ``interacts *only* via the gravitational interaction and *not* through the electromagnetic-, the weak-, or the strong-interaction.'' Therefore, if it did interact via the strong interaction, the name ``dark'' would be unjustified, making Statement D factually false.
\[\boxed{\text{D: f dark matter was known to interact via the strong- interaction, then the epithet "dark" would be justified}}\]
Key points
  • When looking for a false statement in reading comprehension items, look for choices that invert the conditional rules or cause-and-effect relationships explicitly stated in the text.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The line ran ______ the page, right through the centre, and divided the page into two.
questions.explanation:
We need to select the most appropriate preposition to complete the sentence: ``The line ran the page, right through the centre, and divided the page into two.'' Let us analyze the spatial meaning of the choices:
  • across means from one side to the other side of a surface or area. This fits perfectly with a line extending completely from one boundary of a page to the opposite boundary through the center.
  • of expresses possession, origin, or association.
  • between requires exactly two distinct reference objects or landmarks.
  • about denotes proximity, subject matter, or movement in random directions.
Since the action describes a line cutting through a single flat surface space from edge to edge, **across** is the correct preposition. \[\boxed{\text{A. across}}\]
Key points
  • The preposition across describes linear path movement or geometric extension spanning from one side of a continuous two-dimensional plane surface directly to the other.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Kind: ______ :: Often: Seldom (By word meaning)
questions.explanation:
We need to complete the vocabulary analogy by word meaning: \[\text{Kind} : \underline{\hspace{1.5cm}} :: \text{Often} : \text{Seldom}\] Let us analyze the semantic relationship of the baseline reference pair:
  • Often (frequently) and Seldom (rarely) are absolute **antonyms**.
  • Following this identical structural rule, the missing word must function as a direct antonym for the adjective **Kind** (showing a friendly, generous, or considerate nature).
  • The direct opposite of kind among the choices is **A. Cruel** (willfully causing pain or suffering to others).
Evaluating the alternative choices: Variety and Type match the alternative noun definition of kind (as a category) but lack an antonym counterpart in the reference pair, while Kindred means related or similar in kind. \[\boxed{\text{A. Cruel}}\]
Key points
  • Vocabulary analogies require selecting the specific definition branch of a word (e.g., treating kind as an adjective rather than a noun) that maintains a uniform structural relationship across both pairs.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Elvesland is a country that has peculiar beliefs and practices. They express almost all their emotions by gifting flowers. For instance, if anyone gifts a white flower to someone, then it is always taken to be a declaration of one's love for that person.In a similar manner, the gifting of a yellow flower to someone often means that one is angry with that person. Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following sets of statement(s) can be logically inferred with certainty?
  1. In Elvesland, one always declares one's love by gifting a white flower.
  2. In Elvesland, all emotions are declared by gifting flowers.
  3. In Elvesland, sometimes one expresses one's anger by gifting a flower that is not yellow.
  4. In Elvesland, sometimes one expresses one's love by gifting a white flower.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine which sets of statements can be logically inferred with complete text-backed certainty based *only* on the provided passage about Elvesland. Let us evaluate the statements step-by-step using strict textual bounds:
  • Statement (i) claims that one *always* declares love by gifting a white flower. The text only states that ``if anyone gifts a white flower... it is always taken to be a declaration of one's love.'' This conditional rule runs in one direction (\(\text{White Flower} \implies \text{Love}\)). It does **not** mean that a white flower is the *only* way to declare love. Assuming the reverse is the logical fallacy of affirming the consequent. **(Invalid)**
  • Statement (ii) claims *all* emotions are declared by gifting flowers. The passage only notes that they express ``almost all'' their emotions this way, meaning there are exceptions. **(Invalid)**
  • Statement (iii) claims that anger is sometimes expressed by gifting a flower that is *not yellow*. The text states that gifting a yellow flower means one is angry. However, it does **not** state whether other flowers can also express anger, making this claim completely unsupported. **(Invalid)**
  • Statement (iv) states: ``In Elvesland, sometimes one expresses one's love by gifting a white flower.'' Since the text confirms that gifting a white flower is always interpreted as a declaration of love, it is absolutely certain that love is sometimes expressed this way. **(Valid)**
Thus, only statement (iv) can be logically inferred with certainty. This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. only (iv)}}\]
Key points
  • Avoid the logical fallacy of treating a conditional rule (\(A \implies B\)) as a biconditional equivalence (\(A \iff B\)). A single-direction rule only supports existential assertions (``sometimes \(A\) happens'') running in its forward direction.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Based only on the following passage, which one of the options can be inferred with certainty? When the congregation sang together, Apenyo would also join, though her little screams were not quite audible because of the group singing. But whenever there was a special number, trouble would begin; Apenyo would try singing along, much to the embarrassment of her mother. After two or three such mortifying Sunday evenings, the mother stopped going to church altogether until Apenyo became older and learnt to behave. At home too, Apenyo never kept quiet; she hummed or made up silly songs to sing by herself, which annoyed her mother at times but most often made her become pensive. She was by now convinced that her daughter had inherited her love of singing from her father who had died unexpectedly away from home.
options: The mother was embarrassed about her daughter's singing at home.
The mother's feelings about her daughter's singing at home were only of annoyance.
The mother was not sure if Apenyo had inherited her love of singing from her father.
When Apenyo hummed at home, her mother tended to become thoughtful.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the statement that can be logically inferred with complete text-backed certainty based *only* on the provided passage excerpt from *These Hills Called Home*. Let us evaluate the specific behavioral descriptions given in the text:
  • Choice A claims the mother was embarrassed about her singing *at home*, but the text only notes her embarrassment occurred during church services when Apenyo sang along out of tune.
  • Choice B uses the absolute word ``only'', which is unsupported because the text notes her mother felt multiple complex emotions, including becoming pensive.
  • Choice C is incorrect because the text states the mother ``was by now convinced'' of the inheritance, meaning she felt certain about it, not unsure.
  • Choice D states: ``When Apenyo hummed at home, her mother tended to become thoughtful.'' This matches the text perfectly, which explicitly states that when Apenyo hummed or sang to herself at home, it ``annoyed her mother at times but most often made her become pensive.'' Since ``pensive'' is a direct dictionary synonym for being deeply or seriously thoughtful, statement D is factually sound.
\[\boxed{\text{D: When Apenyo hummed at home, her mother tended to become thoughtful.}}\]
Key points
  • Reading comprehension items often test your vocabulary by replacing a descriptive word from the text (such as pensive) with an accurate dictionary synonym (thoughtful) in the correct option choice.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A series of natural numbers \(F_1, F_2, F_3, F_4, F_5, F_6, F_7, \dots\) obeys \(F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1}\) for all integers \(n \ge 2\). If \(F_6 = 37\) and \(F_7 = 60\), then what is \(F_1\)?
questions.explanation:
A series of natural numbers \(F_1, F_2, F_3, \dots\) obeys the second-order linear recurrence relation: \[F_{n+1} = F_n + F_{n-1} \quad \text{for } n \ge 2\] We are given that \(F_6 = 37\) and \(F_7 = 60\). We need to find the value of \(F_3\). Let us work backward from the known higher-order terms using the recurrence subtraction rule \(F_{n-1} = F_{n+1} - F_n\):
  1. Find \(F_5\) by setting \(n = 6\): \[F_7 = F_6 + F_5 \implies 60 = 37 + F_5 \implies F_5 = 60 - 37 = 23\]
  2. Find \(F_4\) by setting \(n = 5\): \[F_6 = F_5 + F_4 \implies 37 = 23 + F_4 \implies F_4 = 37 - 23 = 14\]
  3. Find \(F_3\) by setting \(n = 4\): \[F_5 = F_4 + F_3 \implies 23 = 14 + F_3 \implies F_3 = 23 - 14 = 9\]
  4. Find \(F_2\) by setting \(n = 3\): \[F_2 = F_4 - F_3 \implies F_2=14-9=5\]
  5. Find \(F_1\) by setting \(n = 2\): \[F_1 = F_3 - F_2 \implies F_2=9-5=4\]
Thus, \(F_1 = 4\), which corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 4}}\]
Key points
  • Linear additive recurrence relations (like the Fibonacci sequence) can be solved uniquely in either a forward or backward direction as long as any two consecutive elements are completely specified.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A survey for a certain year found that 90% of pregnant women received medical care at least once before giving birth. Of these women, 60% received medical care from doctors, while 40% received medical care from other healthcare providers. Given this information, which one of the following statements can be inferred with certainty?
options: More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor.
Less than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor.
More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at most once from a doctor.
Less than half of the pregnant women received medical care at most once from a doctor.
questions.explanation:
A survey found that \(90\%\) of pregnant women received medical care at least once before giving birth. Of these women, \(60\%\) received care from doctors, while \(40\%\) received care from other healthcare providers. We need to determine which statement can be inferred with certainty. Let us define the percentages relative to the total population of pregnant women (\(100\%\)):
  • Total receiving care = \(90\%\)
  • Percentage receiving care from a doctor: \[P(\text{Doctor}) = 60\% \text{ of } 90\% = 0.60 \times 90\% = 54\%\]
  • Percentage receiving care from other providers: \[P(\text{Others}) = 40\% \text{ of } 90\% = 0.40 \times 90\% = 36\%\]
Let us evaluate the choices against these calculated values:
  • Choice A states: ``More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor.'' Since \(54\% > 50\%\), this statement is mathematically certain.
\[\boxed{\text{A. More than half of the pregnant women received medical care at least once from a doctor.}}\]
Key points
  • When a percentage is specified as a subset of an intermediate category (e.g., ``60% of *these* women''), multiply the two component percentages directly to find the net share relative to the total grand population.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Looking at the surface of a smooth 3-dimensional object from the outside, which one of the following options is TRUE?
options: The surface of the object must be concave everywhere.
The surface of the object must be convex everywhere.
The surface of the object may be concave in some places and convex in other places.
The object can have edges, but no corners.
questions.explanation:
We are evaluating a smooth, continuous 3-dimensional object from the outside. We need to identify the true statement regarding its geometric curvature properties. Let us analyze the definitions of curvature on a smooth manifold bounding a compact solid:
  • A smooth, closed 3D surface can have localized variations in curvature. It does not need to be uniform across all coordinates. For example, a dumbbell or an hourglass shape features areas that are convex from the outside alongside areas that curve inward (concave regions).
  • Therefore, the surface of the object **may be concave in some places and convex in other places**. This matches statement C perfectly.
  • Note on statement D: A perfectly smooth 3-dimensional object cannot feature sharp edges by definition, as edges introduce discontinuities in the surface normal vectors.
\[\boxed{\text{C. The surface of the object may be concave in some places and convex in other places.}}\]
Key points
  • Smooth surfaces can change their local curvature properties continuously across different regions without breaking differentiability or bounding limits.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The country of Zombieland is in distress since more than 75% of its working population is suffering from serious health issues. Studies conducted by competent health experts concluded that a complete lack of physical exercise among its working population was one of the leading causes of their health issues. As one of the measures to address the problem, the Government of Zombieland has decided to provide monetary incentives to those who ride bicycles to work. Based only on the information provided above, which one of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: All the working population of Zombieland will henceforth ride bicycles to work.
Riding bicycles will ensure that all of the working population of Zombieland is free of health issues.
The health experts suggested to the Government of Zombieland to declare riding bicycles as mandatory.
The Government of Zombieland believes that riding bicycles is a form of physical exercise.
questions.explanation:
We need to find the statement that can be logically inferred with absolute certainty based *only* on the provided text passage. Let us evaluate each choice using strict textual bounds:
  • Choices A and B introduce extreme claims (``All working population...'', ``ensure that all... free of health issues'') which cannot be deduced from a simple incentive policy.
  • Choice C claims the experts suggested making cycling *mandatory*, which contradicts the text stating the government chose to provide *monetary incentives*.
  • Choice D states: ``The Government of Zombieland believes that riding bicycles is a form of physical exercise.'' This is completely logical because the text notes that health experts blamed a ``lack of physical exercise'' for the issues, and the government launched the bicycle program ``as one of the measures to address the problem.''
\[\boxed{\text{D. The Government of Zombieland believes that riding bicycles is a form of physical exercise.}}\]
Key points
  • Logical inference items require identifying the implicit bridge assumption linking the problem cause (lack of exercise) to the policy action (incentivizing bicycle use).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
Consider two functions of time (\(t\)), \(f(t) = 0.01 t^2\) \(g(t) = 4 t\) where \(0 < t < \infty\). Now consider the following two statements:
  • (i) For some \(t > 0\), \(g(t) > f(t)\).
  • (ii) There exists a \(T\), such that \(f(t) > g(t)\) for all \(t > T\).
Which one of the following options is TRUE?
questions.explanation:
We are given two positive functions of time for \(t > 0\): \[f(t) = 0.01t^2, \quad g(t) = 4t\] We need to evaluate the truth value of statements (i) and (ii). Let us find where these two curves intersect by setting \(f(t) = g(t)\): \[0.01t^2 = 4t \implies 0.01t = 4 \implies t = \dfrac{4}{0.01} = 400\] Now, let us analyze the relative behavior of the functions across different time intervals:
  1. Interval 1: For \(0 < t < 400\)
    Let us test \(t = 10\): \(f(10) = 0.01(100) = 1\), and \(g(10) = 4(10) = 40\). Here, \(g(t) > f(t)\). This proves **Statement (i) is TRUE** (since there clearly exist values of \(t > 0\) where \(g(t) > f(t)\)).
  2. Interval 2: For \(t > 400\)
    Let us test \(t = 500\): \(f(500) = 0.01(250000) = 2500\), and \(g(500) = 4(500) = 2000\). Here, \(f(t) > g(t)\). Since the quadratic term \(t^2\) grows faster than the linear term \(t\), \(f(t)\) will remain strictly greater than \(g(t)\) for all values of \(t\) beyond this intersection point (\(T = 400\)). This proves **Statement (ii) is TRUE**.
Since both statements (i) and (ii) are correct, this matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. both (i) and (ii) are correct}}\]
Key points
  • According to asymptotic growth hierarchy laws, any positive quadratic polynomial (\(\mathcal{O}(t^2)\)) will eventually overtake and permanently dominate any linear polynomial (\(\mathcal{O}(t)\)) as \(t\) grows large, regardless of how small its leading coefficient is.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: \(f(x)\) and \(g(y)\) are functions of \(x\) and \(y\), respectively, and \(f(x) = g(y)\) for all real values of \(x\) and \(y\). Which one of the following options is necessarily TRUE for all \(x\) and \(y\)?
questions.explanation:
We are given that \(f(x)\) is a function of \(x\) alone, and \(g(y)\) is a function of \(y\) alone. They satisfy the following equation for all real values of \(x\) and \(y\): \[f(x) = g(y)\] We need to determine what this condition implies about both functions. Let us analyze the independent nature of the variables \(x\) and \(y\):
  1. The left-hand side of the equation, \(f(x)\), depends strictly on \(x\) and cannot vary when \(y\) changes.
  2. The right-hand side of the equation, \(g(y)\), depends strictly on \(y\) and cannot vary when \(x\) changes.
  3. For these two independent functions to remain perfectly equal for any arbitrary choice of \(x\) and \(y\), neither side can change when \(x\) or \(y\) changes.
  4. Therefore, both functions must be identically equal to the exact same fixed scalar constant value: \[f(x) = g(y) = c \quad (\text{where } c \in \mathbb{R})\]
This matches choice B perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{B. } f(x) = g(y) = \text{constant}}\]
Key points
  • Separation of Variables Principle: When an equation uncouples into two separate expressions depending on completely independent variables (\(f(x) = g(y)\)), both expressions must equal a shared constant value.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Which one of the options best describes the transformation of the 2-dimensional figure P to Q, and then to R, as shown?
options: Operation 1: A clockwise rotation by \(90^\circ\) about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure; Operation 2: A reflection along a horizontal line
Operation 1: A counter clockwise rotation by \(90^\circ\) about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure; Operation 2: A reflection along a horizontal line
Operation 1: A clockwise rotation by \(90^\circ\) about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure; Operation 2: A reflection along a vertical line
Operation 1: A counter clockwise rotation by \(180^\circ\) about an axis perpendicular to the plane of the figure; Operation 2: A reflection along a vertical line
questions.explanation:
We need to identify the correct sequence of 2D geometric operations that transforms the asymmetric star figure \(P\) into figure \(Q\), and then into figure \(R\), as shown Let us track the movement of the long extended point of the star across each step:
  1. Operation 1 (From P to Q): In figure \(P\), the longest arm of the star points towards the top-right. In figure \(Q\), this longest arm points towards the bottom-right. This shift represents a **\(90^\circ\) clockwise rotation** about a central axis perpendicular to the plane.
  2. Operation 2 (From Q to R): Let us look at figure \(Q\) and figure \(R\). Notice that the shape has been flipped upside down across a horizontal axis line, which represents a *reflection along a horizontal line*.
Combining these observations matches choice A perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{A}}\]

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A certain country has 504 universities and 25951 colleges. These are categorised into Grades I, II, and III as shown in the given pie charts. What is the percentage, correct to one decimal place, of higher education institutions (colleges and universities) that fall into Grade III?
questions.explanation:
A country has \(504\) universities and \(25,951\) colleges. These are categorized into Grades I, II, and III as shown in the pie charts in. We need to find the combined percentage of higher education institutions that fall into Grade III. Let us calculate the total count of Grade III institutions across both individual categories:
  1. Grade III Universities: The chart shows Grade III represents \(7\%\) of universities: \[N_{U3} = 7\% \text{ of } 504 = 0.07 \times 504 = 35.28\]
  2. Grade III Colleges: The chart shows Grade III represents \(23\%\) of colleges: \[N_{C3} = 23\% \text{ of } 25,951 = 0.23 \times 25,951 = 5968.73\]
Now, sum these parts to find the grand total of Grade III institutions: \[\text{Total Grade III} = N_{U3} + N_{C3} = 35.28 + 5968.73 = 6004.01\] Calculate the total number of higher education institutions in the country: \[\text{Grand Total Institutions} = 504 + 25,951 = 26,455\] Find the total combined percentage: \[\text{Percentage} = \dfrac{6004.01}{26455} \times 100 \approx 22.695\%\] Rounding to one decimal place yields **\(22.7\%\)**, which corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 22.7}}\]
Key points
  • Do not average pie chart sector percentages directly (\(7\% + 23\% \div 2\)) when the baseline sizes of the two groups are completely different. Always calculate the raw counts first before finding the final combined percentage.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: The minute-hand and second-hand of a clock cross each other ____ times between 09:15:00 AM and 09:45:00 AM on a day.
questions.explanation:
We need to find how many times the minute hand and the second hand of a clock cross each other during the specific time interval from 09:15:00 AM to 09:45:00 AM. Let us track the total elapsed duration of this interval: \[\Delta t = 45\text{ minutes} - 15\text{ minutes} = 30\text{ minutes}\] Let us analyze the relative movement of the two hands within a single 1-minute interval:
  • In exactly 1 minute (\(60\text{ seconds}\)), the second hand completes a full \(360^\circ\) circle around the clock face.
  • During that same minute, the minute hand moves forward by a tiny step of exactly 1 minute mark space (\(6^\circ\)).
  • Because the second hand completes a full loop while the minute hand stays relatively stationary, the second hand must pass (cross) the minute hand exactly **once every minute**.
Since there are exactly 30 discrete 1-minute intervals in our 30-minute duration, the second hand will cross the minute hand exactly 30 times. This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 30}}\]
Key points
  • The rapid periodic rotation of the second hand means it crosses the much slower minute hand exactly once during every complete 60-second revolution.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question:
The symbols \(\bigcirc\), \(*\), \(\Delta\) and \(\square\) are to be filled, one in each box, as shown below. The rules for filling in the four symbols are as follows.
  1. Every row and every column must contain each of the four symbols.
  2. Every \(2 \times 2\) square delineated by bold lines must contain each of the four symbols.
Which symbol will occupy the box marked with '?' in the partially filled figure?
questions.explanation:
We are given a \(4 \times 4\) grid puzzle with four symbols: \(\bigcirc, *, \Delta, \square\). The rules are:
  1. Every row and every column must contain each of the four symbols.
  2. Every \(2 \times 2\) block outlined by bold lines must contain each of the four symbols.
We need to determine which symbol replaces the question mark ? located at **Row 1, Column 2**. Step 1: Analyze the top-left \(2 \times 2\) block The top-left \(2 \times 2\) block occupies:
  • (Row 1, Col 1), (Row 1, Col 2 [?])
  • (Row 2, Col 1), (Row 2, Col 2 [\(\bigcirc\)])
Since each \(2 \times 2\) block must contain all four symbols, the ? cell cannot be \(\bigcirc\). Thus, ? \(\in \{*, \Delta, \square\}\). Step 2: Check Row 1 and Column 2 constraints
  • Row 1 analysis: Row 1 already contains \(\Delta\) at Column 4. Therefore, ? cannot be \(\Delta\).
  • Column 2 analysis: Column 2 already contains \(\bigcirc\) (Row 2) and an empty space, but let us look at the top-right \(2 \times 2\) block:
    • Row 1, Col 4 \(= \Delta\)
    • Row 2, Col 3 \(= *\)
    In Row 2, the symbols present are \(\bigcirc\) (Col 2) and \(*\) (Col 3). In Row 2, Col 4: Row 4, Col 4 \(= \bigcirc\) and Row 3, Col 4 \(= *\), so Col 4 has \(\Delta\) (Row 1), \(*\) (Row 3), \(\bigcirc\) (Row 4). This means Row 2, Col 4 must be \(\square\).
  • Row 2, Col 1: Since Row 2 has \(\bigcirc\), \(*\), and \(\square\), the remaining symbol for Row 2, Col 1 is \(\Delta\).
  • Top-Left \(2 \times 2\) block evaluation:
    The top-left \(2 \times 2\) block now contains:
    • Row 2, Col 1 \(= \Delta\)
    • Row 2, Col 2 \(= \bigcirc\)
    Row 1, Col 1 sits in Column 1. Column 1 already has \(*\) at Row 4. Thus, Row 1, Col 1 cannot be \(*\), which means Row 1, Col 1 must be \(*\). Therefore, the remaining symbol in the top-left \(2 \times 2\) block for ? (Row 1, Col 2) is \(\square\).
This corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. } \square}\]
Key points
  • Sudoku grid puzzles are resolved by systematically checking row, column, and quadrant boundaries to eliminate symbols that already appear along those intersecting lines.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Consider the following inequalities: \(p^2 - 4q < 4\) \(3p + 2q < 6\) where \(p\) and \(q\) are positive integers. The value of \((p+q)\) is _____.
questions.explanation:
We are given two simultaneous inequalities where \(p\) and \(q\) are strictly **positive integers** (\(p, q \in \{1, 2, 3, \dots\}\)): \[\begin{aligned} \text{(1)} \quad p^2 - 4q &< 4 \\ \text{(2)} \quad 3p + 2q &< 6 \end{aligned}\] We need to find the value of the expression \((p + q)\). Let us isolate the possible values for our variables using inequality (2) first: \[3p + 2q < 6 \implies 3p < 6 - 2q\] Since \(p\) and \(q\) must be positive integers, let us test the lowest possible integer value for \(q\), which is \(q = 1\): \[3p < 6 - 2(1) \implies 3p < 4 \implies p < \dfrac{4}{3} \approx 1.33\] The only positive integer strictly less than \(1.33\) is **\(p = 1\)**. Let us verify if higher values of \(q\) are possible. If \(q \ge 2\): \[3p < 6 - 2(2) \implies 3p < 2 \implies p < \dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.67\] Since no positive integer is less than \(0.67\), \(q\) cannot be greater than or equal to 2. Thus, the only possible integer solution is **\(p = 1\) and \(q = 1\)**. Let us verify if this pair satisfies inequality (1): \[p^2 - 4q = (1)^2 - 4(1) = 1 - 4 = -3\] Since \(-3 < 4\), inequality (1) is satisfied perfectly. Now, calculate our target value: \[p + q = 1 + 1 = 2\] This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 2}}\]
Key points
  • Diophantine systems with inequality bounds are solved quickly by testing the smallest possible integers for the variables. This rapidly narrows down the search space and isolates the unique valid root.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: How many pairs of sets (S, T) are possible among the subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} that satisfy the condition that S is a subset of T?
questions.explanation:
We need to find the total number of unique pairs of sets \((S, T)\) chosen from the subsets of a 6-element master set \(M = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\) that satisfy the condition: \[S \subseteq T\] Let us analyze the placement choices available for any single element \(x\) belonging to the master set \(M\):
  • For the condition \(S \subseteq T\) to hold true, each element \(x\) can fall into exactly one of three mutually exclusive regions:
    1. Element \(x\) is inside set \(S\), which means it must also be inside set \(T\) (\(x \in S\) and \(x \in T\)).
    2. Element \(x\) is outside set \(S\), but inside set \(T\) (\(x otin S\) and \(x \in T\)).
    3. Element \(x\) is completely outside both sets \(S\) and \(T\) (\(x otin S\) and \(x otin T\)).
  • Notice that an element can **never** be inside \(S\) but outside \(T\), because that would violate our subset rule (\(S \subseteq T\)).
Thus, every single element in the master set has exactly **3 unique placement choices**. Since the master set contains \(n = 6\) independent elements, we find the total number of valid set combinations using the product rule: \[ ext{Total Pairs } (S, T) = 3^n = 3^6 = 729\] This matches choice A perfectly. \[ oxed{ ext{A. 729}}\]
Key points
  • For any nested subset configuration involving \(k\) nested layers (\(A_1 \subseteq A_2 \subseteq \dots \subseteq A_k \subseteq M\)), each element has exactly \(k+1\) placement choices. Thus, the total number of combinations is given by \((k+1)^n\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: An opaque pyramid shown below, with a square base and isosceles faces, is suspended in the path of a parallel beam of light, such that its shadow is cast on a screen oriented perpendicular to the direction of the light beam. The pyramid can be reoriented in any direction within the light beam. Under these conditions, which one of the shadows P, Q, R and S is NOT possible?
questions.explanation:
An opaque regular pyramid with a square base and isosceles triangular faces is suspended in a parallel beam of light. Its shadow is cast onto a screen oriented perpendicular to the beam. We need to identify which silhouette shape among P, Q, R, and S is **NOT possible** to form by reorienting the pyramid. Let us analyze the possible 2D orthographic projections of a square-based pyramid from different viewing angles:
  • View from directly underneath the base: Projects a perfect **Square (S)**.
  • View directly from the side (face-on): Projects a symmetric **Isosceles Triangle (R)**.
  • View from an angled, tilted perspective: As the pyramid tilts relative to the light beam, the flat base edges and apex combine to project various multi-sided asymmetric polygons, such as a **Kite-like Quadrilateral (P)**.
  • Evaluating Shape Q: Shape Q shows an asymmetric shape with sharp, narrow extended parallel points that cannot be formed by projecting the straight boundary generators of a simple convex regular pyramid.
Therefore, shadow silhouette Q is impossible to form. This matches choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B}}\]
Key points
  • Convex Projection Rule: The shadow cast by a convex 3D solid under a parallel beam of light will always be a convex 2D polygon. Shapes with reflex internal angles or non-linear curves cannot be formed.

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: Given a fair six-faced dice where the faces are labelled `1', `2', `3', `4', `5', and `6', what is the probability of getting a `1' on the first roll of the dice and a `4' on the second roll?
questions.explanation:
We are rolling a fair six-faced die twice independently. We need to find the probability of getting a '1' on the first roll and a '4' on the second roll. Let us analyze the individual probabilities for each independent event:
  • A standard fair die contains 6 equally likely outcomes: \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\}\).
  • Probability of rolling a '1' on the first roll: \(P(E_1) = \dfrac{1}{6}\)
  • Probability of rolling a '4' on the second roll: \(P(E_2) = \dfrac{1}{6}\)
Since these consecutive rolls are completely independent events, the combined probability of both outcomes happening in sequence is found using the probability multiplication rule: \[P(E_1 \cap E_2) = P(E_1) \times P(E_2) = \dfrac{1}{6} \times \dfrac{1}{6} = \dfrac{1}{36}\] This calculation corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 1/36}}\]
Key points
  • Independent Events Rule: For any two independent events, the probability of both events happening concurrently or sequentially is the product of their individual probabilities: \(P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \cdot P(B)\).

questions.subject: general-aptitude
questions.question: A recent survey shows that 65% of tobacco users were advised to stop consuming tobacco. The survey also shows that 3 out of 10 tobacco users attempted to stop using tobacco. Based only on the information in the above passage, which one of the following options can be logically inferred with certainty?
options: A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco made an attempt to do so.
A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco did not attempt to do so.
Approximately 30% of tobacco users successfully stopped consuming tobacco.
Approximately 65% of tobacco users successfully stopped consuming tobacco.
questions.explanation:
We are given two facts about a sample of tobacco users:
  • \(65\%\) of tobacco users were advised to stop consuming tobacco.
  • \(3\) out of \(10\) tobacco users (\(30\%\)) attempted to stop using tobacco.
We need to determine which statement can be logically inferred with certainty. Step 1: Define the subsets in terms of total users (\(N\))
  • Let \(A\) be the set of users who were advised to stop: \(|A| = 0.65 N\).
  • Let \(T\) be the set of users who attempted to stop: \(|T| = 0.30 N\).
Step 2: Determine the intersection and overlap
Consider the group \(A \cap T\) (users who were advised AND attempted to stop):
  • The maximum possible number of advised users who attempted to stop occurs when all users who attempted were also advised (\(T \subseteq A\)).
  • In this best-case scenario, \(|A \cap T| = 0.30 N\).
Step 3: Analyze advised users who DID NOT attempt to stop
  • Out of the \(65\%\) who were advised, at most \(30\%\) of the total user population could have made an attempt.
  • Therefore, the minimum percentage of advised users who did not attempt to stop is: \[0.65 N - 0.30 N = 0.35 N \quad (35\% \text{ of total users})\]
  • Expressed as a proportion of the advised group (\(A = 65\%\)): \[\text{Fraction of advised users who did not attempt} \ge \dfrac{35\%}{65\%} \approx 53.85\%\]
  • Since \(53.85\% > 50\%\), a **majority** (\(>50\%\)) of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco definitely did not attempt to do so.
Step 4: Evaluate the options
  1. Option A: At most \(30\% / 65\% \approx 46.15\%\) of advised users attempted to stop, which is a minority (\(\le 50\%\)). Thus, False.
  2. Option B: At least \(53.85\%\) of advised users did not attempt to stop, which constitutes a strict majority. Thus, **True with certainty**.
  3. Options C & D: The text discusses attempts made, not successful outcomes. Thus, uninferable.
This corresponds to choice B. \[\boxed{\text{B. A majority of tobacco users who were advised to stop consuming tobacco did not attempt to do so.}}\]
Key points
  • Avoid making assumptions when evaluating separate datasets (e.g., people who received advice vs. people who tried to quit) unless the text explicitly states the overlap or connection between them.

  • There are exactly 5 horizontal-ish lines (including the top and bottom boundaries).
  • There are exactly 5 vertical-ish lines (including the left and right boundaries).
  • There is 1 continuous diagonal line connecting opposite corners.
Each unique pairing of a horizontal line and a vertical line forms an intersection point that defines the potential vertex of a triangle completed by the diagonal line. The total number of such intersections is: \[5 \times 5 = 25 \text{ points}\] However, because the diagonal line passes exactly through the main grid intersections, there are exactly 5 points where a horizontal line, a vertical line, and the diagonal line all intersect at a single concurrent point. At these 5 points, the enclosed area is zero, so no triangle is formed. Subtracting these 5 non-enclosed points from the total number of intersections yields: \[\text{Total Triangles} = 25 - 5 = 20\] This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 20}}\]

questions.question: The digit in the unit's place of the product \(3^{999} \times 7^{1000}\) is
questions.explanation:
We need to find the digit in the unit's place of the massive product expression: \[P = 3^{999} \times 7^{1000}\] Let us find the unit digit pattern for each base factor using the principle of **modular cyclicity**: Step 1: Find the unit digit of \(3^{999}\)
The unit digits of powers of 3 repeat in a cycle of 4: \([3, 9, 7, 1]\). To find where 999 fits in this cycle, divide the exponent by 4 and find the remainder: \[999 \pmod 4 = 3\] The 3rd value in the power cycle of 3 is **7**: \[3^{999} \equiv 7 \pmod{10}\] Step 2: Find the unit digit of \(7^{1000}\)
The unit digits of powers of 7 also repeat in a cycle of 4: \([7, 9, 3, 1]\). Divide this exponent by 4 and find the remainder: \[1000 \pmod 4 = 0 \quad (\text{exactly divisible})\] A remainder of 0 corresponds to the 4th value in the cycle, which is **1**: \[7^{1000} \equiv 1 \pmod{10}\] Step 3: Multiply the unit digits together
Now, multiply the two individual unit digits to find the final result: \[\text{Final Unit Digit} = (7 \times 1) \pmod{10} = 7\] This matches choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 7}}\]
Key points
  • The unit digits of integer powers repeat in periodic cycles of at most 4 steps. You can find the unit digit of any large power easily by evaluating its exponent modulo 4 (\(n \pmod 4\)).

questions.question: What is the smallest number with distinct digits whose digits add up to 45?
questions.explanation:
We need to find the **smallest number** with **distinct digits** whose digits add up to \(45\). Let us analyze the mathematical constraints to minimize the numerical value of an integer:
  1. To make a number as small as possible, we must first **minimize its total number of digits**.
  2. The largest possible value we can get by summing single, distinct non-zero digits is by adding all 9 base decimal digits together: \[1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 + 8 + 9 = 45\]
  3. Since we must use exactly these 9 distinct digits to reach the sum of 45, any valid number must be a 9-digit number.
  4. To minimize the value of a 9-digit number, we must arrange these digits in **ascending order** from left to right, placing the smallest digits in the highest place-value positions (leftmost positions).
Sorting the digits \(\{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9\}\) in ascending order yields the value: **\(123456789\)**. This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 123456789}}\]
Key points
  • Value Optimization Rule: To find the smallest possible number matching a fixed digit sum, minimize the total digit count first, then arrange the digits in strictly ascending order from left to right.

questions.question:
In a class of 100 students,
  1. there are 30 students who neither like romantic movies nor comedy movies,
  2. the number of students who like romantic movies is twice the number of students who like comedy movies, and
  3. the number of students who like both romantic movies and comedy movies is 20.
How many students in the class like romantic movies?
questions.explanation:
In a class of \(100\) students, let \(R\) be the set of students who like romantic movies, and let \(C\) be the set of students who like comedy movies. We are given the following parameters:
  • Total population \(N = 100\)
  • Students who like neither: \(|R' \cap C'| = 30 \implies\) Total who like at least one category: \[|R \cup C| = 100 - 30 = 70\]
  • Intersection (like both categories): \(|R \cap C| = 20\)
  • Relative ratio: \(|R| = 2|C|\)
Using the principle of inclusion-exclusion for overlapping sets: \[|R \cup C| = |R| + |C| - |R \cap C|\] Substitute our known values into this equation: \[70 = |R| + |C| - 20 \implies |R| + |C| = 90\] Now, substitute the ratio condition \(|C| = \dfrac{|R|}{2}\) into the sum equation: \[|R| + \dfrac{|R|}{2} = 90 \implies \dfrac{3|R|}{2} = 90\] \[3|R| = 180 \implies |R| = 60\] Therefore, the number of students who like romantic movies is exactly 60. This matches choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 60}}\]
Key points
  • Venn diagram word problems are solved efficiently by isolating the union group (\(|R \cup C|\)) and using inclusion-exclusion principles to substitute relative proportions.

questions.question:
Out of 1000 individuals in a town, 100 unidentified individuals are covid positive. Due to lack of adequate covid-testing kits, the health authorities of the town devised a strategy to identify these covid-positive individuals. The strategy is to:
  1. Collect saliva samples from all 1000 individuals and randomly group them into sets of 5.
  2. Mix the samples within each set and test the mixed sample for covid.
  3. If the test done in (ii) gives a negative result, then declare all the 5 individuals to be covid negative.
  4. If the test done in (ii) gives a positive result, then all the 5 individuals are separately tested for covid.
Given this strategy, no more than ______ testing kits will be required to identify all the 100 covid positive individuals irrespective of how they are grouped.
questions.explanation:
A town has a population of \(1000\) individuals, out of which exactly \(100\) individuals are Covid-positive. The health authorities use a sample pooling strategy to identify all positive individuals:
  1. The 1000 individual samples are divided into sets of 5 (\(\frac{1000}{5} = 200\) total pools).
  2. Each pooled sample is tested. If a pool tests positive, all 5 individuals in that pool are re-tested separately.
We need to calculate the maximum number of testing kits required to identify all positive individuals under the **worst-case scenario**. Let us calculate the total number of tests step-by-step:
  1. Phase 1 (Initial Pool Testing):
    Every single one of the 200 pools must be tested initially: \[N_{\text{phase1}} = 200 \text{ tests}\]
  2. Phase 2 (Individual Re-testing in Positive Pools):
    To maximize the total number of tests required, we look at the worst-case scenario where the \(100\) positive individuals are distributed across as many different pools as possible.
    • Since each pool can hold multiple positive individuals, distributing the 100 positive cases across separate pools means that exactly **100 pools** will turn out positive.
    • Each of these 100 positive pools triggers individual testing for all 5 members in that pool: \[N_{\text{phase2}} = 100 \text{ pools} \times 5 \text{ tests/pool} = 500 \text{ tests}\]
Now, sum the tests from both phases to find the maximum total number of testing kits required: \[\text{Total Tests} = N_{\text{phase1}} + N_{\text{phase2}} = 200 + 500 = 700\] This matches choice A perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{A. 700}}\]
Key points
  • Group Testing Optimization: In sample pooling problems, the worst-case maximum test count happens when the positive cases are spread out as much as possible across separate pools. This forces the maximum number of groups to trigger individual follow-up testing.

questions.question: A \(100 \text{ cm} \times 32 \text{ cm}\) rectangular sheet is folded 5 times. Each time the sheet is folded, the long edge aligns with its opposite side. Eventually, the folded sheet is a rectangle of dimensions \(100 \text{ cm} \times 1 \text{ cm}\). The total number of creases visible when the sheet is unfolded is _____.
questions.explanation:
We are given a rectangular sheet of dimensions \(100\text{ cm} \times 32\text{ cm}\). The sheet is folded \(5\) times such that each fold aligns the long edge (\(100\text{ cm}\)) with its opposite side, halving the short dimension (\(32\text{ cm}\)) every time while leaving the long dimension unchanged (\(100\text{ cm}\)). Step 1: Track dimensions and folds along the \(32\text{ cm}\) side
  • Initial dimension: \(32\text{ cm}\)
  • After Fold 1: \(32 / 2 = 16\text{ cm}\)
  • After Fold 2: \(16 / 2 = 8\text{ cm}\)
  • After Fold 3: \(8 / 2 = 4\text{ cm}\)
  • After Fold 4: \(4 / 2 = 2\text{ cm}\)
  • After Fold 5: \(2 / 2 = 1\text{ cm}\)
This results in the final rectangle of dimensions \(100\text{ cm} \times 1\text{ cm}\), confirming that all \(5\) folds were made parallel to the \(100\text{ cm}\) edge along the \(32\text{ cm}\) side. Step 2: Calculate total visible creases Folding a paper in half \(n\) times in one direction divides that dimension into \(2^n\) equal segments. The number of crease lines required to divide a sheet into \(2^n\) parallel strip segments is: \[\text{Total Creases} = 2^n - 1\] Substitute \(n = 5\): \[\text{Total Creases} = 2^5 - 1 = 32 - 1 = 31\] This corresponds to choice C. \[\boxed{\text{C. 31}}\]

questions.question: A `frabjous' number is defined as a 3 digit number with all digits odd, and no two adjacent digits being the same. For example, 137 is a frabjous number, while 133 is not. How many such frabjous numbers exist?
questions.explanation:
A ``frabjous'' number is defined as a 3-digit number where all its digits are odd, and no two adjacent digits are the same. We need to find how many such numbers exist. Let us analyze the available digit options from the standard decimal system:
  • The set of available odd digits is: \(S = \{1, 3, 5, 7, 9\} \quad (\text{Total of 5 elements})\).
Let us calculate the choices for each position of a 3-digit number (\(\underline{D_1} \, \underline{D_2} \, \underline{D_3}\)) from left to right:
  1. Hundreds Digit (\(D_1\)): Can be filled using any of the 5 odd digits in set \(S\): \[\text{Choices for } D_1 = 5\]
  2. Tens Digit (\(D_2\)): Cannot be equal to the adjacent hundreds digit (\(D_2 \neq D_1\)). This eliminates exactly 1 digit from our choices, leaving: \[\text{Choices for } D_2 = 5 - 1 = 4\]
  3. Units Digit (\(D_3\)): Cannot be equal to its adjacent tens digit (\(D_3 \neq D_2\)). It is allowed to be equal to \(D_1\) because they are not adjacent. This again eliminates exactly 1 digit, leaving: \[\text{Choices for } D_3 = 5 - 1 = 4\]
Using the fundamental product rule of combinatorics, we multiply the independent choices together: \[\text{Total Frabjous Numbers} = 5 \times 4 \times 4 = 80\] This matches choice D perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{D. 80}}\]
Key points
  • Adjacency Constraint Rule: For sequences where adjacent elements cannot repeat, the number of choices for the first position equals the total size of the set (\(m\)), while every subsequent position has exactly \(m-1\) choices, regardless of previous choices.

questions.question: Which one among the following statements must be TRUE about the mean and the median of the scores of all candidates appearing for GATE 2023?
options: The median is at least as large as the mean.
The mean is at least as large as the median.
At most half the candidates have a score that is larger than the median.
At most half the candidates have a score that is larger than the mean.
questions.explanation:
We need to identify which mathematical statement must be TRUE regarding the mean and median scores of candidates appearing for a large competitive examination like GATE 2023. Let us evaluate the choices using fundamental statistical definitions:
  • The median of any dataset represents the exact 50th percentile mark when the data points are sorted in order. By definition, at most half (\(\le 50\%\)) of the population can have a value strictly greater than the median, and at least half must fall at or below it. This makes Statement C mathematically certain.
  • Statements A and B are incorrect because the relative values of the mean and median depend heavily on the skewness of the test score distribution. In highly skewed distributions, either value can be larger.
  • Statement D is incorrect because if a distribution has a long right tail (positive skew), the mean can be significantly larger than the median, meaning far less than half of the candidates will score above the mean.
\[\boxed{\text{C. At most half the candidates have a score that is larger than the median.}}\]
Key points
  • The median acts as a strict percentile separator. Unlike the mean, which is sensitive to outliers, the median splits a population dataset such that the proportion of points lying strictly above it can never exceed 50%.

questions.question:
Ankita has to climb 5 stairs starting at the ground, while respecting the following rules:
  1. At any stage, Ankita can move either one or two stairs up.
  2. At any stage, Ankita cannot move to a lower step.
Let \(F(N)\) denote the number of possible ways in which Ankita can reach the \(N^{th}\) stair. For example, \(F(1)=1\), \(F(2)=2\), \(F(3)=3\). The value of \(F(5)\) is ________.
questions.explanation:
Ankita needs to climb a flight of 5 stairs (\(N = 5\)) starting from the ground (\(N = 0\)). She must follow two movement rules:
  1. At any stage, she can move up by either 1 stair or 2 stairs.
  2. She can never move downward.
Let \(F(N)\) represent the total number of unique ways she can reach the \(N^{\text{th}}\) stair. We want to find the value of \(F(5)\). Let us analyze the choice Ankita faces at the very last step to reach the \(N^{\text{th}}\) stair:
  • She could have arrived by taking a 1-stair step from the previous stair (\(N-1\)). The number of ways to do this is \(F(N-1)\).
  • Or, she could have arrived by taking a 2-stair step from two stairs below (\(N-2\)). The number of ways to do this is \(F(N-2)\).
Summing these two mutually exclusive possibilities gives the classic Fibonacci recurrence relation: \[F(N) = F(N-1) + F(N-2)\] We are given the initial baseline values: \(F(1) = 1\) and \(F(2) = 2\). Let us calculate the values sequentially up to \(N = 5\):
  • For \(N = 3\): \(F(3) = F(2) + F(1) = 2 + 1 = 3 \quad (\text{Given in problem context})\)
  • For \(N = 4\): \(F(4) = F(3) + F(2) = 3 + 2 = 5\)
  • For \(N = 5\): \(F(5) = F(4) + F(3) = 5 + 3 = 8\)
Thus, there are exactly 8 unique ways to climb the 5 stairs, which corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 8}}\]
Key points
  • Path counting problems with a choice of steps of size 1 or 2 always map directly onto the Fibonacci recurrence sequence \(F(N) = F(N-1) + F(N-2)\).

questions.question:
The information contained in DNA is used to synthesize proteins that are necessary for the functioning of life. DNA is composed of four nucleotides: Adenine (A), Thymine (T), Cytosine (C), and Guanine (G). The information contained in DNA can then be thought of as a sequence of these four nucleotides: A, T, C, and G. DNA has coding and non-coding regions. Coding regions---where the sequence of these nucleotides are read in groups of three to produce individual amino acids---constitute only about 2% of human DNA. For example, the triplet of nucleotides CCG codes for the amino acid glycine, while the triplet GGA codes for the amino acid proline. Multiple amino acids are then assembled to form a protein. Based only on the information provided above, which of the following statements can be logically inferred with certainty?
  1. The majority of human DNA has no role in the synthesis of proteins.
  2. The function of about 98% of human DNA is not understood.
questions.explanation:
We need to determine which statement can be logically inferred with certain validity based *only* on the provided text passage regarding DNA coding and protein synthesis. Let us analyze the text parameters carefully:
  • Statement (i) claims that a majority of human DNA has no role in protein synthesis. The text states that coding regions (which produce amino acids) make up ``only about 2% of human DNA.'' This means the remaining \(98\%\) consists of non-coding regions. However, the text does not state that non-coding DNA has ``no role'' in protein synthesis; it simply states that they are non-coding regions. Therefore, (i) cannot be inferred with certainty.
  • Statement (ii) claims that the function of about \(98\%\) of human DNA is not understood. The text says that \(98\%\) of DNA consists of non-coding regions, but it does not say that scientists do not understand their function. Saying a region is non-coding is a description of its structure, not a statement that its function is a mystery. Therefore, (ii) cannot be inferred with certainty.
Since neither statement (i) nor statement (ii) can be inferred with text-backed certainty, choice D is the correct option. \[\boxed{\text{D. neither (i) nor (ii)}}\]
Key points
  • Strict reading comprehension rules forbid equating a technical description (like ``non-coding DNA'') with a lack of scientific knowledge (``not understood'') unless the text explicitly states that connection.

questions.question: Which one of the given figures P, Q, R and S represents the graph of the following function? \[f(x)=||x+2|-|x-1||\]
questions.explanation:
We need to find which graph (P, Q, R, or S) correctly represents the multivariable piecewise absolute function: \[f(x) = \Big| |x + 2| - |x - 1| \Big|\] Let us find the behavior of the inner function, \(g(x) = |x + 2| - |x - 1|\), by evaluating it across three distinct real intervals defined by its critical roots (\(x = -2\) and \(x = 1\)):
  1. Interval 1: For \(x \le -2\)
    Both absolute terms inside have negative arguments: \[g(x) = -(x + 2) - \left[ -(x - 1) \right] = -x - 2 + x - 1 = -3\] Applying the outer absolute value: \(f(x) = |-3| = 3\). This means the graph forms a flat horizontal line at \(y = 3\) for all values to the left of \(x = -2\).
  2. Interval 2: For \(x \ge 1\)
    Both absolute terms inside have positive arguments: \[g(x) = (x + 2) - (x - 1) = x + 2 - x + 1 = 3\] Applying the outer absolute value: \(f(x) = |3| = 3\). This means the graph forms a flat horizontal line at \(y = 3\) for all values to the right of \(x = 1\).
  3. Interval 3: For intermediate values \(-2 < x < 1\)
    The first argument is positive, while the second remains negative: \[g(x) = (x + 2) - \left[ -(x - 1) \right] = x + 2 + x - 1 = 2x + 1\] Applying the outer absolute value: \(f(x) = |2x + 1|\). This linear function has a root where \(2x + 1 = 0 \implies x = -0.5\). At this point, the curve drops down to touch the x-axis (\(f(-0.5) = 0\)), forming a sharp V-shaped valley between \(x = -2\) and \(x = 1\).
Let us compare this piecewise behavior to our options:
  • Graph P displays flat plateaus at \(y = 3\) on both outer ends (\(x \le -2\) and \(x \ge 1\)) and features a V-shaped valley that drops to zero at \(x = -0.5\). This matches our derived functions perfectly.
This corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. P}}\]
Key points
  • Piecewise absolute value functions are solved efficiently by analyzing the intervals defined by their critical roots. Finding the flat boundary plateaus on the outer edges lets you quickly eliminate incorrect graph shapes.

questions.question: An opaque cylinder is suspended in the path of a parallel beam of light, such that its shadow is cast on a screen oriented perpendicular to the direction of the light beam. The cylinder can be reoriented in any direction within the light beam. Under these conditions, which one of the shadows P, Q, R, and S is NOT possible?
questions.explanation:
An opaque solid cylinder is suspended in a parallel beam of light. Its shadow is cast onto a flat screen oriented perpendicular to the direction of the light beam. We need to identify which shadow shape among P, Q, R, and S is NOT possible to form by reorienting the cylinder in 3D space. Let us analyze the possible 2D orthographic projections of a cylinder from different angles:
  • View from directly face-on (parallel to circular base): The projection along the longitudinal axis forms a perfect Circle (P).
  • View from directly side-on (perpendicular to longitudinal axis): The rectangular cross-section projects as a perfect sharp Rectangle (R).
  • View from an angled, tilted perspective: As the cylinder tilts relative to the parallel light beam, the flat circular ends project as curved ellipses, while the straight side walls remain parallel. This forms a stadium-like shape with rounded caps and flat sides, which matches Shape Q.
  • Evaluating Shape S: Shape S is a parallelogram with sharp, skewed corner angles. Because a cylinder's cross-section contains perfectly circular circular boundaries, tilting it can only generate smooth elliptical curves or perpendicular straight lines. It is physically impossible for a cylinder to project sharp, non-perpendicular corner angles like a parallelogram.
Therefore, shadow silhouette S is impossible to form, which corresponds to choice D. \[\boxed{\text{D. S}}\]
Key points
  • Orthographic Projection Rule: Smooth, curved 3D solids cannot project flat shadows with sharp, non-perpendicular skewed angles (like a parallelogram) because geometric transformations preserve the continuity of smooth surface normal vectors.

questions.question: In the given figure, PQRS is a parallelogram with PS=7 cm, PT=4 cm and PV=5 cm. What is the length of RS in cm? (The diagram is representative.)

We are given a parallelogram \(PQRS\) with side length \(PS = 7\text{ cm}\) and two perpendicular altitudes dropped from vertex \(P\): \(PT = 4\text{ cm}\) (perpendicular to base \(QR\)) and \(PV = 5\text{ cm}\) (perpendicular to base \(RS\)). We need to find the length of side \(RS\). Let us utilize the invariant property of geometric area computation for a parallelogram: \[\text{Area} = \text{Base} \times \text{Corresponding Height}\]
  1. Using base \(QR\): In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal in length, so \(QR = PS = 7\text{ cm}\). The corresponding height dropped to this base is \(PT = 4\text{ cm}\): \[\text{Area} = QR \times PT = 7 \times 4 = 28\text{ cm}^2\]
  2. Using base \(RS\): The corresponding height dropped to this side base is \(PV = 5\text{ cm}\): \[\text{Area} = RS \times PV = RS \times 5\]
Since both equations calculate the exact same total area of parallelogram \(PQRS\), we equate the two expressions: \[RS \times 5 = 28 \implies RS = \dfrac{28}{5}\text{ cm}\] This matches choice B perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{B. 28/5}}\]
Key points
  • The total area of a polygon is a geometric scalar invariant. Setting area equations from two different base-altitude orientations equal to each other allows you to quickly calculate a missing side length.

questions.question: To construct a wall, sand and cement are mixed in the ratio of 3:1. The cost of sand and that of cement are in the ratio of 1:2. If the total cost of sand and cement to construct the wall is 1000 rupees, then what is the cost (in rupees) of cement used?
questions.explanation:
To construct a wall, sand and cement are mixed together. We are given the following ratio parameters:
  • Ratio of the quantity/volume of materials used: \(Q_{\text{sand}} : Q_{\text{cement}} = 3 : 1\)
  • Ratio of the unit cost of materials: \(P_{\text{sand}} : P_{\text{cement}} = 1 : 2\)
  • Total overall cost of the construction mixture = Rs. \(1000\)
We need to calculate the total amount spent specifically on cement. Let us introduce scalar multipliers to express the individual quantities and unit prices: \[Q_{\text{sand}} = 3x, \quad Q_{\text{cement}} = 1x\] \[P_{\text{sand}} = 1y, \quad P_{\text{cement}} = 2y\] Now, write the cost equation for each component by multiplying its quantity by its unit price:
  • Total expenditure on sand: \(C_{\text{sand}} = 3x \times 1y = 3xy\)
  • Total expenditure on cement: \(C_{\text{cement}} = 1x \times 2y = 2xy\)
Sum these individual expenses to find the total overall cost of the wall: \[C_{\text{total}} = C_{\text{sand}} + C_{\text{cement}} = 3xy + 2xy = 5xy\] We are given that the total cost is Rs. 1000: \[5xy = 1000 \implies xy = \dfrac{1000}{5} = 200\] Finally, calculate the total cost spent on cement (\(C_{\text{cement}}\)): \[C_{\text{cement}} = 2xy = 2 \times 200 = 400\text{ Rs.}\] This corresponds to choice A. \[\boxed{\text{A. 400}}\]
Key points
  • Total component cost allocations are determined by finding the product of their volume ratio and their unit price ratio (\(\text{Total Cost} \propto \text{Quantity} \times \text{Unit Price}\)).

questions.question: The coefficient of \(x^{4}\) in the polynomial \((x-1)^{3}(x-2)^{3}\) is equal to ________.
questions.explanation:
We need to find the coefficient of the \(x^4\) term in the product expansion of the polynomial: \[P(x) = (x - 1)^3 (x - 2)^3\] First, combine the two separate cubed terms into a single expression using exponential exponent distribution laws (\(a^n b^n = (ab)^n\)): \[P(x) = \left[ (x - 1)(x - 2) \right]^3 = \left[ x^2 - 3x + 2 \right]^3\] Now, expand this trinomial cube expression using the general multinomial expansion theorem, or by factoring out terms sequentially: \[\left[ x^2 - 3x + 2 \right]^3\] Let us find all unique combinations of the inner terms that multiply together to form an \(x^4\) power term:
  • The general expansion form is \(\sum \dfrac{3!}{i!j!k!} (x^2)^i (-3x)^j (2)^k\), where indices must sum to 3 (\(i + j + k = 3\)).
  • We want the net power of \(x\) to be 4, which means \(2i + j = 4\). Let us solve for the valid integer combinations:
    1. Case 1: Let \(i = 2 \implies 2(2) + j = 4 \implies j = 0\). Since \(i+j+k=3\), we find \(k = 3 - 2 - 0 = 1\). The coefficient for this combination is: \[\dfrac{3!}{2!0!1!} \times (1)^2 \times (-3)^0 \times (2)^1 = 3 \times 1 \times 1 \times 2 = 6\]
    2. Case 2: Let \(i = 1 \implies 2(1) + j = 4 \implies j = 2\). Finding the remaining index: \(k = 3 - 1 - 2 = 0\). The coefficient for this combination is: \[\dfrac{3!}{1!2!0!} \times (1)^1 \times (-3)^2 \times (2)^0 = 3 \times 1 \times 9 \times 1 = 27\]
Summing the coefficients from both valid cases gives: \[\text{Total Coefficient of } x^4 = 6 + 27 = 33\] This matches choice A perfectly. \[\boxed{\text{A. 33}}\]
Key points
  • Simplify matching higher-order polynomial products by combining shared powers first: \((x-1)^3(x-2)^3 = [(x-1)(x-2)]^3\). You can then find specific coefficients quickly by listing the valid integer index sets under the multinomial theorem constraints.
